#5086. Monero’s Delisting Nightmare Continues: XMR Price Plunges 15%

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Data from BitInfoCharts shows that Monero fell from $525.36 to $446.54 during Thursday’s trading session. For longtime XMR investors, the sell-off is an uncomfortable reminder of what happened when Binance announced its Monero delisting in February 2024.

This time, however, the list of major exchanges available to Monero traders is considerably shorter.

In a November 26 announcement, KuCoin confirmed that it will remove all four Monero spot trading pairs against USDT, USDC, ETH and BTC on November 30 at 08:00 UTC.

The exchange has already suspended XMR deposits and does not intend to reopen them. Withdrawals are scheduled to remain available until December 31 at 08:00 UTC, although KuCoin reserves the right to close them earlier if problems affecting the network arise.

Monero’s removal extends beyond spot trading. KuCoin will discontinue XMR flexible savings on November 27, followed by its conversion and automated trading services on November 30.

There is another detail in the announcement that deserves particular attention. KuCoin will stop accepting XMR as collateral for its VIP loan products. Customers who have borrowed against their Monero holdings may need to provide alternative collateral to avoid liquidation.

For holders planning to leave their coins on the exchange until the withdrawal deadline, KuCoin also warned that remaining balances could be converted into stablecoins, although “such conversion is not guaranteed.”

The exchange cited its platform policies but did not identify a specific regulatory requirement behind the decision.

KuCoin is not the first exchange to abandon Monero this month, but its departure could prove particularly significant given the amount of XMR trading it handles.

A November 26 snapshot from CoinGecko identified KuCoin as Monero’s most active exchange, with its XMR/USDT pair recording approximately $62.6 million in trading volume over a 24-hour period.

Earlier this month, MEXC discontinued spot trading for Monero on November 17. Binance removed the cryptocurrency in February 2024, while Kraken halted XMR trading for European Economic Area customers in October of the same year, explicitly citing regulatory changes.

Trading volume does not simply disappear when an exchange delists an asset. Some of it will move elsewhere, and investors who intend to keep their holdings can withdraw them to private wallets.

The bigger question is how efficiently the remaining exchanges can absorb that activity. If fewer venues are competing for the same orders, particularly during periods of market stress, large trades could become more expensive to execute and price swings more pronounced.

For Monero, that is increasingly a market structure problem rather than a question of whether its underlying technology works.

There is a case against assuming that Thursday’s sell-off marks the beginning of a prolonged decline.

Monero has survived previous exchange removals and even managed to establish new price highs in 2026 despite mounting restrictions. As NewsBTC previously reported, XMR traded above $700 earlier this year, long after Binance stopped supporting its spot markets.

But a functioning network does not guarantee a liquid market. Investors still need practical ways to enter and exit their positions without incurring excessive trading costs.

November 30 will therefore be an important test for Monero. Rather than focusing solely on whether XMR recovers the $500 level, traders should watch where KuCoin’s trading volume migrates and whether the remaining exchanges can absorb larger orders without substantial slippage.

That will offer a better indication of whether Thursday’s decline was a temporary reaction to another delisting or a warning of a deeper liquidity problem.

#5085. Bank of Japan Warns Stablecoins and Tokenization Threaten Financial Stability

Japan's central bank has warned that automated trading in tokenized markets could exacerbate a sell-off.

It also raised concerns about whether stablecoin holders can always redeem their tokens at face value.

A Bank of Japan executive director outlined these risks during his keynote speech at an International Monetary Fund seminar in Tokyo.

In the event of a price drop, according to Kazushige Kamiyama, a smart contract could automatically increase the amount of collateral required. It could also trigger a sale of the collateral backing a position if the borrower doesn't have enough collateral.

These sales could drive prices even lower, potentially spreading financial stress across institutions and markets.

In the case of stablecoins, the question is whether a token with a face value of one dollar can always be redeemed for one dollar.

To ensure this, issuers' reserves need to be properly regulated, and the links to central bank money need to be reliable, Kamiyama said.

A bank might have enough cash to pay for a trade in tokenized assets but still be unable to complete the payment.

This could happen when a trade is settled overnight, and the payment system the bank uses to transfer cash is unavailable.

The bank might have to keep additional cash on a trading platform. Meanwhile, cash held on another network might not be accessible when the payment is due.

"Even with faster settlement, it does not necessarily lead to efficient liquidity management," Kamiyama said.

Cross-border securities trades, however, could benefit from tokenization.

A smart contract could link the payment and delivery of a security so that both transactions are executed simultaneously.

This could reduce the risk of a buyer paying for an asset without receiving it.

The Bank of Japan is setting up a testing environment with financial institutions that hold accounts at the central bank.

One scenario involves exploring how cash settlement could work for trades involving tokenized Japanese government bonds.

The central bank is considering two options for making the cash payment.

One would involve issuing tokenized central bank money. The other would link a token trading platform to Japan's existing payment infrastructure.

These tests will evaluate whether the proposed solutions can address the challenges financial institutions face when settling trades.

#5084. Michael Saylor’s Net Worth Plunges $6 Billion: The Cost of His Bitcoin Bet

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Michael Saylor’s net worth has fallen by approximately $6 billion since the cryptocurrency market peaked in October 2025. The Strategy co-founder, whose fortune was estimated at $9.3 billion at the time, is now worth around $3.3 billion, according to Forbes.

The decline has wiped out nearly two-thirds of Saylor’s estimated wealth. Yet the billionaire’s company continues to accumulate Bitcoin despite mounting paper losses, showing little willingness to reconsider its investment strategy.

For Saylor, the downturn presents a problem that extends well beyond the price of Bitcoin. Much of his fortune depends on a company that must convince investors to keep financing its accumulation strategy.

Saylor was already among the cryptocurrency industry’s biggest financial casualties in February, when Forbes estimated that his wealth had fallen by $4.7 billion from its October 2025 level.

His fortune briefly stabilized in the following months, reaching an estimated $4.7 billion in June, before suffering another setback.

The latest estimate puts Saylor’s wealth approximately 64.5% below its October 2025 level.

Bitcoin’s return to the $60,000 level has added pressure, but the cryptocurrency alone does not explain the scale of the decline. Saylor’s exposure through Strategy makes his financial position considerably more complicated than that of an ordinary Bitcoin investor.

The $6 billion represents a reduction in estimated wealth, not a confirmed cash loss or the proceeds of any disclosed asset sales.

In October 2020, Saylor disclosed that he personally owned 17,732 BTC, acquired for approximately $175 million.

At the Bitcoin price of $60,325 reported by Strategy on November 26, those holdings would be worth approximately $1.07 billion, assuming he still owns the entire disclosed amount.

That would leave his original personal investment with an unrealized gain of roughly $895 million.

His current personal Bitcoin balance has not been independently confirmed, but the calculation illustrates an important distinction. Saylor can lose billions in estimated wealth while remaining substantially profitable on his original Bitcoin purchases.

The situation at Strategy is quite different.

While Saylor began buying Bitcoin at considerably lower prices, his company has spent much of the past several years increasing its exposure at higher valuations.

According to its November 23 SEC filing, Strategy acquired another 457 BTC for $29.6 million, bringing its total holdings to 851,305 BTC.

The company has spent approximately $64.23 billion accumulating Bitcoin at an average purchase price of $75,446.

Its official Bitcoin dashboard valued those reserves at approximately $51.35 billion on November 26.

That leaves a gap of nearly $12.9 billion between the company’s cumulative acquisition cost and the market value of its Bitcoin holdings.

These figures do not represent realized trading losses, nor do they capture the full financial performance of the company.

Nevertheless, the numbers reveal how dramatically the economics of accumulating Bitcoin have changed during the downturn.

For years, investors were willing to pay a premium for Strategy shares. The attraction was not simply the Bitcoin it owned, but the prospect that management could raise additional capital and increase shareholders’ exposure to the cryptocurrency.

That premium is no longer something the company can take for granted.

Strategy’s dashboard showed an mNAV ratio of 0.94 at the November 25 stock market close, using its own net Bitcoin value per share methodology.

The company’s latest investor briefing acknowledges the implications:

A widening discount can cause MSTR to underperform BTC even when bitcoin rises.

This is where Saylor’s investment model faces a more difficult test.

When investors are willing to pay a premium for Strategy shares, raising capital to acquire more Bitcoin can improve the economics of the business. When that premium disappears, issuing additional shares becomes a more complicated proposition.

Strategy’s own sensitivity analysis shows that a Bitcoin price of $40,000 would reduce its estimated net reserve value per share to $45.37, compared with $163.17 at a Bitcoin price of $100,000. The figures illustrate how sensitive the company’s underlying reserve valuation is to Bitcoin price movements.

Strategy’s third-quarter financial results offer a clearer picture of why its cash reserves and financing obligations now matter almost as much as the price of Bitcoin.

Buying more Bitcoin is only one part of the equation. The cost of financing those purchases matters just as much.

There is a credible case for recovery. Strategy still owns more than 850,000 Bitcoin, giving it considerable exposure to any sustained cryptocurrency market rebound.

The company also reported approximately $4.82 billion in combined cash and dollar reserves in its latest investor briefing, providing a buffer against its financing obligations.

But a recovery in Bitcoin would not necessarily produce an equivalent recovery in Saylor’s wealth. Strategy’s share price also depends on its debt, preferred-stock obligations, access to capital and the valuation investors are willing to assign to its business model.

The next test for Saylor is not whether he can buy another thousand Bitcoin. It is whether he can continue financing those purchases on terms that benefit existing shareholders.

His personal fortune has already demonstrated how expensive that distinction can become.

#5083. Chainlink jumps 10% as its Wall Street ambitions gain momentum on two fronts

Fidelity is expanding investment access to LINK as Chainlink develops the infrastructure to keep tokenized financial markets operating around the clock.

Chainlink's LINK token climbed 10% over the past 24 hours to $9.20 as the network deepened its integration with traditional finance.

The rally comes as Fidelity Investments filed to launch a spot Chainlink exchange-traded fund (ETF), a day after enabling direct LINK trading on its cryptocurrency platform.

Meanwhile, Chainlink has expanded its financial market data infrastructure to support round-the-clock trading and lending involving tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets, including during market holidays such as Thanksgiving.

On Nov. 25, Fidelity submitted a registration statement to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for its proposed Fidelity Chainlink Fund, which would trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

The fund would hold LINK directly, with Anchorage Digital, BitGo and Coinbase Custody safeguarding its assets. It would support cash and in-kind share creations and redemptions but would not stake its underlying tokens.

The filing came a day after Fidelity added LINK, AAVE and UNI to its Fidelity Crypto platform, expanding its customers' access to digital assets.

While eligible Fidelity Crypto customers can now purchase LINK directly, the proposed ETF would extend that access to investors seeking exposure through conventional brokerage accounts.

The consecutive moves could substantially broaden LINK's investor base. Fidelity serves approximately 57 million individual investors and reported $7.9 trillion in managed assets and $20.1 trillion in assets under administration at the end of September, making it one of the largest financial services firms in the US.

However, Fidelity is entering a market where investor appetite has weakened considerably.

According to SoSoValue data, Grayscale and Bitwise's spot Chainlink ETFs have attracted $176 million in cumulative net inflows since their respective launches. However, the funds recorded net inflows for just one day in November, putting them on course for their first month of net withdrawals since the market's inception.

Daily net flows for GLNK and CLNK through Nov. 25. Values follow Maketo's displayed rounding and totals are approximate, and non-trading days are excluded.

The slowdown in demand, coupled with LINK's price decline, has reduced the funds' combined net assets by approximately 33%, from $238.2 million at the end of September to $158.6 million on Nov. 25.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Fidelity's extensive retail and financial advisory network could help revive demand, but limited fresh capital could also intensify competition among issuers.

With Fidelity yet to disclose its management fee or launch date, the terms of its offering could determine how effectively it competes with Grayscale and Bitwise for LINK investors.

Beyond expanding investment access to LINK, Chainlink is positioning its infrastructure to capture growing demand for financial markets that operate outside traditional exchange hours.

On Nov. 26, the decentralized oracle network introduced Chainlink 24/7 on its X account, a market data service that extends pricing coverage for traditional financial assets to weekends and public holidays.

The service builds on Chainlink's existing 24/5 infrastructure, which provides pricing for more than $1.6 billion in tokenized equities across six blockchains and supports platforms including Ondo, xStocks, Robinhood, and Coinbase.

Previously, blockchain-based financial applications struggled to value traditional assets when their underlying markets closed, limiting trading opportunities and complicating collateral management.

Chainlink's new service addresses that gap by combining traditional market data during active trading sessions with perpetual-futures-derived pricing when exchanges are closed.

The infrastructure could support continuous trading in tokenized assets, derivatives, and prediction markets, while letting decentralized lending protocols manage collateral risks outside conventional market hours.

Aave, which had more than $34 billion in total value locked at the service's launch, is adopting the infrastructure through Horizon, its institutional lending platform, initially targeting tokenized US equities.

The expansion also affects LINK's economics.

Fidelity's ETF prospectus identifies demand for Chainlink's services as a factor influencing LINK's value, noting that the network converts certain fees paid in fiat currencies and other digital assets into LINK through its Payment Abstraction mechanism.

While Fidelity's expansion creates another avenue for investment demand, Chainlink's ability to generate additional fee-paying activity from always-on financial markets could provide a separate source of demand for its token.

Home » Blitz news » New EU Crypto Sanctions Extend SWIFT’s Russia Blockade

The Commission just granted a multi-faceted sanction package going ham on Russia’s various uses of crypto.

The European Commission’s 22nd sanctions package against Russia extends the European Union’s (EU) transaction ban to over 60 Russian banks and says all 60 of those will be removed from SWIFT, President Ursula von der Leyen said in Strasbourg on 23 November 2026.

This comes just weeks after Russia officially legalized crypto currency trading, starting with the big-cap coins like Bitcoin (BTC) & Ethereum (ETH). In the 22nd sanction packet, Russian-linked crypto services & platforms were specifically named as banned for transactions.

“The measures include the possibility for EU firms to sue their non-Russian contractual parties in the EU to recover damages.”, – states the document. “We will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine”, further said the Chief Commissioner.

With this package, we are increasing the pressure.We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms.We are further isolating Russia. We are shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events.… pic.twitter.com/9Ltkpohylq

While focusing on Russian SWIFT sanctions, the EU added 51 entities to the anti-circumvention list, while the majority of them, 27, were outside Russia: 14 came from China, including four in Hong Kong, four in Türkiye, three in Kyrgyzstan, two in India, two in Kazakhstan and two more in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

The European Union (EU) freshly assembled the Crypto Task Force to counter new crypto-related ways of evading the huge pile of sanctions, including limitations of Russian business abroad via ‘third-world’ parties. The Council will decide when the ban enters into force, after the necessary measures are activated.

#5080. Ethereum’s Co-Founder Takes On Crypto’s Next Security Threat. Who Is Vitalik Buterin?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Who is Vitalik Buterin, and why is Ethereum’s co-founder now questioning the security of the very devices crypto investors use to protect their wealth? The 32-year-old programmer has turned his attention to a problem that even open-source software cannot necessarily solve: compromised computer chips.

In an essay published on November 26, Buterin argued that cryptocurrency security needs to extend beyond software and into the physical hardware on which it runs. His message builds on one of crypto’s oldest principles, but with a new twist:

For someone who helped build an alternative to centralized financial infrastructure, questioning the manufacturers behind that infrastructure seems like a natural next step.

Vitalik Buterin is a Russian-Canadian programmer, researcher and writer who conceived Ethereum in 2013, at the age of 19.

Born in Russia in 1994 and raised in Canada, Buterin discovered Bitcoin in 2011. He went on to co-found Bitcoin Magazine, where he explored the technology and economics behind cryptocurrencies long before digital assets attracted mainstream financial institutions.

His involvement in Bitcoin exposed him to a problem that would eventually lead to Ethereum. Blockchain technology had potential beyond transferring money, but building more sophisticated applications on Bitcoin presented technical limitations.

Rather than trying to accommodate every possible application within Bitcoin’s existing architecture, Buterin began working on a blockchain designed specifically for programmability.

At the time, he was studying computer science at the University of Waterloo, where he also worked as a research assistant to cryptographer Ian Goldberg.

According to the University of Waterloo, Buterin received a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship in 2014 and subsequently left university to work on Ethereum full-time.

In November 2013, Buterin wrote the initial draft of what would become the Ethereum whitepaper.

The proposal described a blockchain with a general-purpose programming environment. Developers would no longer need to create an entirely new network every time they wanted to build a decentralized application.

Consider a lending platform. Instead of relying on a bank to manage collateral, calculate interest and authorize withdrawals, developers could encode those rules into smart contracts running on Ethereum.

That does not eliminate every risk. Smart contracts can contain bugs, depend on unreliable external data or operate under centralized administrative controls. What Ethereum introduced was the ability to execute financial and other programmable agreements on a shared blockchain.

Although Buterin originated the concept, Ethereum was not built by him alone. Its founding team included seven other individuals: Gavin Wood, Joseph Lubin, Charles Hoskinson, Anthony Di Iorio, Mihai Alisie, Jeffrey Wilcke and Amir Chetrit.

The project’s first live network, known as Frontier, launched on July 30, 2015.

What began as an experimental computing platform eventually became the foundation for much of the decentralized finance industry. Stablecoins, decentralized exchanges, lending protocols and tokenized financial assets now use the infrastructure that Buterin and Ethereum’s early contributors helped establish.

The network’s own evolution, particularly its transition to proof-of-stake and the development of Layer 2 scaling networks, has shaped Ethereum’s first decade.

A hardware wallet is supposed to keep private keys away from potentially compromised computers and smartphones. But what happens if the device itself cannot be trusted?

Buterin’s latest research examines that possibility. He points to supply chain attacks involving tampered wallets and considers the potential for malicious modifications concealed inside apparently legitimate chips.

Open-source firmware allows researchers to examine the instructions a device runs. But those instructions reveal little about whether the manufactured chip has been altered.

Buterin wants manufacturers to disclose physical chip layouts, known as GDS files, so investigators have a reference against which to inspect actual hardware.

The distinction matters. Knowing what a chip is designed to do is not necessarily the same as knowing what the chip inside your wallet actually does.

One approach highlighted by Buterin comes from hardware security researcher Andrew Huang, better known as bunnie.

Huang has been developing a technique called Infra-Red, In Situ inspection (IRIS), which exploits the fact that silicon becomes transparent at certain infrared wavelengths.

Using infrared illumination and suitable imaging equipment, researchers can examine parts of a chip’s internal structure without necessarily removing it from its circuit board.

The technique could help detect substituted components or unexpected differences between manufactured chips and their intended designs.

In a 2024 update on his research, Huang explained that infrared imaging has resolution limits. It cannot reliably reveal every microscopic feature of modern chips. Combining imaging with additional electrical testing could improve confidence in a component’s integrity.

That is an important limitation for crypto investors. Publishing an open hardware design does not automatically make a wallet secure, just as publishing a smart contract’s code does not establish that it is free of vulnerabilities.

Buterin acknowledges that sophisticated hardware inspections are more likely to be performed by specialist organizations than ordinary wallet owners.

His essay is a proposal for improving security, not an announcement that existing hardware wallets have all been compromised.

Despite his status as Ethereum’s most recognizable co-founder, Buterin is not its CEO.

Ethereum is maintained through the participation of independent developers, researchers, node operators, validators and other ecosystem contributors. Changes to the network involve technical proposals, discussion, software development and adoption by participants.

Buterin has considerable influence over those discussions, but publishing a proposal does not give him the authority to implement it unilaterally.

His role within the Ethereum Foundation is also distinct from control over the blockchain itself. In its April 2025 governance announcement, the Foundation described Buterin’s responsibilities as providing technical and intellectual guidance to the wider ecosystem.

His research can influence the direction Ethereum takes. Whether the network ultimately follows that direction depends on considerably more than his endorsement.

Buterin accumulated considerable wealth through his involvement in Ethereum, with much of his publicly visible cryptocurrency wealth tied to ETH.

However, his exact net worth is not publicly established.

Blockchain analytics can estimate the value of assets held in wallets attributed to him, but those figures do not necessarily account for all his investments, liabilities, private assets or holdings at addresses that have not been publicly identified.

They also fluctuate with cryptocurrency prices. A wallet valuation should therefore not be confused with a complete assessment of his personal wealth.

Buterin’s latest essay is part of a longer-running interest in making digital infrastructure independently verifiable.

In September 2025, he published The Importance of Full-Stack Openness and Verifiability, exploring how transparency could extend across the hardware and software underpinning increasingly important parts of people’s lives.

These interests share a practical concern: whether users can independently establish that the systems they rely on behave as intended.

There is a commercial obstacle, though. Semiconductor manufacturers invest heavily in proprietary processes, and designing chips specifically for inspectability can involve performance compromises.

But a device signing a cryptocurrency transaction does not necessarily need the computing power of a modern AI processor. That makes security-focused hardware a potentially useful starting point.

More than a decade ago, Buterin challenged the idea that blockchains should primarily be used to transfer money. His latest work challenges another assumption the industry has grown comfortable with: that trusting the code is enough.

For crypto investors, the next meaningful development may come from hardware manufacturers willing to make their products independently inspectable, rather than another software update promising greater security.

#5079. LayerZero locks early ZRO deposits behind validators users cannot choose

LayerZero’s launch validators will share the voting power of early ZRO deposits, with withdrawals locked until 2027.

LayerZero named Kakao Pay and ZAN among the first validators for its Zero blockchain on Nov. 25 and said Four Pillars would run validator operations on behalf of Samsung Card.

The operators are slated to help confirm blocks when Zero opens to the public, a launch planned for Nov. 30.

The appointments show who will exercise some of the voting weight tied to early deposits of ZRO, the token that backs validator votes on Zero.

Under LayerZero’s staking terms, the portal automatically spreads early stake equally across the initial validators. Holders have no say in which validators receive it and no way to withdraw early.

LayerZero says its launch validators will span Asia, Europe and North America. Its Nov. 25 announcement names the Asia-Pacific participants and identifies Four Pillars as the operator for Samsung Card.

Validators check proofs that transactions were processed correctly and vote on blocks. A validator’s vote carries more weight when more ZRO is staked behind it, according to LayerZero’s staking guide.

The project’s February technical paper describes a design in which operators can validate without putting up their own tokens, and the network selects its consensus committee in proportion to stake.

The portal’s rewards calculator shows 300 million ZRO in an illustrative scenario that assumes 30% participation.

A holder who disagrees with a validator during the lock has no option in the portal to redirect the stake or exit the position, and the lock covers the staked tokens and any rewards.

LayerZero expects unstaking to open by March 31, 2027, and says that date may change. Once unstaking opens, it can take up to seven days, so moving ZRO off Zero to another chain may require a later upgrade.

LayerZero describes a 1% annual issuance target as the basis for the reward pool, and the terms set an initial validator commission of 10% on rewards. A holder’s share depends on how much ZRO they stake, how long they stake it, and how much others commit.

Any rewards compound into the locked position, and the staking guide says validators will set their own commission after the initial period.

Until unstaking opens, stakers can track their balances, but the selected validator set exercises the consensus votes backed by those deposits. The public launch is the next chance to see which of the announced validators come online.

Given that this is a good start, bulls can keep an eye on NEAR token‘s progress. $3.47 will be the pivotal level that would signal a credible bullish trend shift.

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Why XRP Analysts Flag $8.30 Macro Price Target

Two recent posts have put long-term XRP price projections back in view. One centers on a multi-year chart pattern with an $8.30 target, while the other argues that full replacement of SWIFT would support valuations above $15,000. XRP is trading near $0.95.

#XRP – The $8.30 Number 🎯:This remains one of my most powerful macro charts.The original white symmetrical triangle breakout target has STILL not been reached.What if everything happening right now is simply the macro retest of that breakout before the real expansion?My… pic.twitter.com/F0tdM5mxtl

XRP remains well below its 2025 high near $3.65, and the pattern’s interpretation is subject to debate among traders.

A separate post by Ripple_Mino claimed that if XRP fully replaces SWIFT, the token could be valued beyond $15,000. The argument rests on XRP’s divisibility: one XRP equals one million drops, so even extreme valuations would still allow practical fractional use.

When XRP replaces Swift, it will be valued beyond $15,000 per token.The original token design allowed for such a valuation as 1 XRP can be divided into 1,000,000 smaller units known as drops.So 1 Drop = 0.000001 XRP(one millionth of an XRP) pic.twitter.com/WcBEPSh0XA

Official and recent developments do not support the premise of XRP’s SWIFT replacement.

SWIFT has launched its own blockchain-based shared ledger for tokenized bank deposits, with more than a dozen major banks participating in trials. SWIFT has not announced any integration of XRP as a settlement asset for that system.

Former SWIFT innovation leadership has publicly rejected claims of XRP integration, and the network continues to emphasize its own infrastructure and tokenized deposits rather than a single external token.

The $8.30 figure is a technical target drawn from a multi-year chart structure, while the $15,000 figure is a hypothetical based on a scenario that SWIFT and major participating banks haven’t endorsed yet.

Neither projection is reflected in current market pricing yet or officially top-confirmed institutional commitments. XRP’s price action continues to trade well below both levels as of late November 2026.

The link between SWIFT as a traditional financial intermediary and XRP’s native chain comes multi-layered, with intersection across liquidity provision and instant settlement environments.

#5076. XRP sellers could lose an extra $3,146 on a large trade if five accounts pull their buy orders

Removing five accounts’ buy orders in a simulation cut sampled XRP market depth by 86% and large-sale proceeds by 3.3%.

Five XRP Ledger accounts supplied 72% of one day’s trading volume in XRP against Ripple USD (RLUSD), according to XRPL.to.

For a test of the next day’s order book, CryptoSlate selected the five addresses that led the Nov. 25 session in fills of at least 1,000 XRP, then simulated removing their buy orders.

Funded RLUSD in the first 100 buy offers fell from about 63,925 to 8,805. In the model, the matching pool, a standing reserve of both assets, took most of a 100,000 XRP sale after the removal. A seller would receive about 3.3% less RLUSD than with the full sample.

The last XRP/USD trade on Kraken was $0.94935 when the ticker was checked at 13:07:24 UTC on Nov. 26. On the ledger exchange itself, XRP/RLUSD accounted for 84% of all volume measured in XRP over the seven days covered by XRPL.to’s reconstruction.

In the 24 hours ending at 01:30 UTC on Nov. 25, XRPL.to’s reconstruction counted 25,801 fills moving about 6.3 million XRP. Traders took resting offers from 142 accounts or traded against the automated pool.

The biggest account, whose ledger address starts with rpiFwLYi, supplied 41% of executed volume. Together, the five largest supplied 72%, and the pool accounted for 3%.

A replay through the public trade history endpoint yielded 6.32 million XRP and counted 25,712 fills for the same window, 89 fewer than the published tally.

The index can group multiple executions into one transaction row. In one row covering 525.58 XRP, the validated transaction showed about 514 tokens went to one account’s buy orders and about 12 tokens to another’s.

To test whether concentration persisted, CryptoSlate used XRPL.to records and split combined fills using validated ledger changes.

The comparison covered same-pair fills of at least 1,000 XRP in three 24-hour windows ending at 01:30 UTC on Nov. 24, 25 and 26. The same five addresses, selected by Nov. 25 qualifying volume, accounted for about 71%, 88%, and 79% of qualifying volume, respectively.

The address starting with rpiFwLYi led the middle session, with about half the qualifying volume. An address starting with rURtT5MM led the sessions on either side.

That left the same group with a large share in all three windows even as the leading address changed, and the turnover includes trades in which the addresses gave or received XRP.

The two sides of the XRP Ledger’s order book draw on different inventories. A resting order to buy XRP is funded in RLUSD, which the seller receives. A resting order to sell XRP draws on the seller’s inventory.

The relevant depth for a seller is the RLUSD that buyers can deliver at the displayed prices.

At validated ledger 108584374, which closed at 13:09:20 UTC on Nov. 26, the first 100 buy offers could take about 67,549 XRP at the displayed prices.

Excluding buy offers from the five large-fill leaders left room for about 9,302 XRP in that same sample. The funded RLUSD in the sample fell about 86%.

The matching XRP/RLUSD pool held about 1.99 million XRP and 1.89 million RLUSD. The model applied its standard 0.315% fee and allocated each portion of the sale to the better available price.

The test held the remaining offers fixed and used only the sampled book and the direct pool, with deeper orders, replacement orders, and additional fees outside the simulation.

In the model, a 1,000 sale returned 947.96 RLUSD with the full order sample and 947.87 without the five addresses’ buy orders. At 10,000, proceeds slipped from 9,474.85 to 9,470.90 RLUSD. At 100,000, proceeds fell from 94,197.18 to 91,050.74 RLUSD.

The pool took about 32,451 XRP in the first case and 90,698 after the orders were removed.

#5072. HRF Announces Funding of Seven Bitcoin Projects for People Living Under Authoritarian Regimes

Together, these efforts help human rights defenders, journalists, nonprofits, and individuals hold, send, and verify their money freely under repression.

HRF’s grantees for Round III of 2026 are:

Many people want to self-custody bitcoin, but in much of the world, buying a hardware wallet is too expensive. CryoBrick transforms feature phones into offline Bitcoin signing devices. Because it looks and works like an ordinary phone, activists living under authoritarian regimes can self-custody bitcoin while maintaining plausible deniability. Technical Director Apalok will use HRF’s support to conduct comprehensive security hardening and peer review, integrate Bitchat for offline messaging, and publish how-to guides, expanding access to bitcoin and the property rights it protects to a far larger global user base.

Bitcoin’s benefits remain out of reach for many African communities because high-quality education resources do not exist in their local languages. Exonumia, an open-source project that translates Bitcoin educational content, is building a Bitcoin Glossary in 21 African languages. The project will coordinate a continent-wide community of translators through three in-person and 12 virtual translation sprints, where native speakers review and validate more than 250 terms. Because every term is validated by native speakers rather than machines, the approved terms give wallet developers a trustworthy foundation for localizing bitcoin software into African languages, extending access to bitcoin education and the financial freedom it offers. HRF’s support will see the glossary published as a free public resource.

In much of Africa, democratic elections remain a struggle and most countries are not fully free. Exacerbating this, evidence of fraud documented by citizens is often lost because paper forms go missing and photos and messages cannot be verified. Pawavox, created by Nigerian civic-tech founder Jason Omu, is a platform that gives election observers and human rights defenders a new way to record irregularities. Using Pawavox, observers capture short video or voice reports, each GPS-tagged and timestamped. This evidence is then published to Nostr, a decentralized communications protocol, as a record that is much harder for anyone to tamper with. HRF’s grant will help fund the completion of the Nostr integration and expansion across Africa, helping protect the integrity of the evidence on which democratic accountability depends.

Branded hardware wallets are a common way to self-custody bitcoin, but under repressive regimes, they can be expensive and attract unwanted attention. SeedSigner is an open-source signing device that users assemble themselves from inexpensive, widely available parts, so there is no finished-device supply chain for an attacker to compromise. It currently runs on a small computer, called a Raspberry Pi Zero, which can be unavailable in regions that need self-custody most. Lead maintainer Keith Mukai will use HRF’s support to migrate the SeedSigner code to more widely available hardware, ending dependence on any single manufacturer. Then, more individuals under repressive regimes will be able to hold their own bitcoin without trusting anyone else.

Nigeria is one of the world’s most active digital asset markets, but the legal path to acquiring bitcoin runs through exchanges that collect troves of identity and transactional data. At the same time, many rural Nigerian homes are receiving solar electricity for the first time, but much of that power goes unused in the daytime. Strandedwatt, a bitcoin mining initiative, installs small open-source Bitcoin miners in homes, converting surplus solar power into bitcoin, which is paid privately and directly to host households. The next step, backed by HRF, will see Bitnob CEO and project lead Bernard Parah deploy 100 Jua Kali miners in these homes and publish an open-source playbook other communities can replicate. Meanwhile, households excluded by the Nigerian financial system gain a permissionless path to freedom money.

A commercial Bitcoin hardware wallet has software and hardware the user cannot inspect, and carrying one can signal to outsiders that someone owns bitcoin. Specter DIY is a fully open-source, air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet that anyone can build from off-the-shelf components and verify line by line. There is no purchase record, and the finished device does not look like a Bitcoin wallet at all. For activists in Belarus, dissidents in Venezuela, and journalists in Burma, it is a path to financial self-sovereignty. HRF’s grant to the Specter Association, the nonprofit that maintains the project, helps fund hardware costs, AI tooling, and vulnerability bounties, ensuring the developers behind a self-custody tool dissidents can inspect and verify remain supported.

#5071. Morpho’s largest euro stablecoin vault is €13.8 million short of covering its biggest depositor’s exit

Morpho’s largest EURCV vault faces a 13.8 million EURCV liquidity shortfall if its biggest depositor seeks a full exit.

Morpho’s largest listed vault for EUR CoinVertible (EURCV), a euro stablecoin, showed about 13.8 million EURCV less liquidity than its biggest address would need for a full exit on Nov. 26.

A withdrawal would return EURCV to a wallet, but eligible holders seeking euros directly from issuer SG-FORGE would follow a separate redemption timetable.

Morpho’s Steakhouse Prime EURCV vault on Ethereum showed 144.3 million EURCV in deposits and 107.2 million in displayed liquidity, including tokens the app could pull from other lending markets.

The top address accounted for 121 million EURCV (83.8%), according to the same page. Steakhouse Prime was the largest EURCV vault by assets in Morpho’s public ranking.

The comparison assumes the top address sought to withdraw its entire position at that moment. Morpho’s public data show balances by address, which can pool funds for more than one owner.

The European Banking Authority’s Nov. 25 report on stablecoins in decentralized finance found that, in its July analysis, more than half of circulating EURCV was supplied to a Morpho vault.

A standard vault withdrawal draws on idle tokens and funds that can be pulled from the market designated for withdrawals. At Ethereum block 26,500,641, Morpho’s address-level position data put that route’s limit at 103.1 million EURCV against a position worth 120.99 million.

That left about 17.9 million EURCV beyond the ordinary withdrawal limit at the indexed block.

Under Morpho’s withdrawal rules, the app can pull available funds from other markets when the vault configuration allows it, a process called forced deallocation.

Morpho’s withdrawal-options data showed about 102.8 million EURCV idle and about $340,000 available in the designated market, plus about 4 million that could be pulled from other markets, based on rounded amounts.

That last source of funds explains why the app showed more liquidity than a standard withdrawal could use. What a depositor can withdraw depends on what is still available when the transaction executes.

In a lending market where borrowers are using most of the funds, repayments or fresh deposits can free up tokens for another withdrawal.

On eligible vaults, Morpho also offers an in-kind exit that can return some EURCV to the wallet and convert part of the redeemed amount into a direct position in a lending market.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Two Nov. 26 liquidity readings show how much of the largest position the vault could cover in a hypothetical full exit.

Vault liquidity controls how many tokens can leave. Direct issuer redemption has its own eligibility checks and cash deadline.

The app view and indexed ordinary withdrawal limit are separate Nov. 26 readings. The issuer path applies to eligible EEA residents under the September 2026 white paper, subject to checks and transfer requirements. A submitted withdrawal may face changed liquidity.

Draw bars on a shared zero-based scale using rounded millions of EURCV. The app comparison subtracts 107.22 million of displayed liquidity from 120,991,559.56 EURCV of position value, rounded to 13.77 million. Morpho’s same-day position API supplies the ordinary limit, which excludes forced deallocation. The indexed gap is 120.99 million minus 103.13 million, using the same block.

The app view and indexed ordinary withdrawal limit are separate Nov. 26 readings. The issuer path applies to eligible EEA residents under the September 2026 white paper, subject to checks and transfer requirements. A submitted withdrawal may face changed liquidity.

SG-FORGE’s September 2026 EURCV white paper says holders resident in the European Economic Area can request direct redemption at one euro per token.

The issuer applies identity, anti-money-laundering, sanctions and other checks, and may require the holder to transfer the tokens to it.

SG-FORGE says it will transfer euros to the holder’s cash account by the last business day of the month after the checks clear. For example, if the checks clear in December, the white paper’s timetable sets the payment deadline for the last business day of January.

#5069. The 12 Best Swim Trunks for Men of 2026, Worn and Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our editors recommend shorts from Rhone and Fair Harbor.

SUMMER MAY BE behind us, but that doesn’t mean your swim trunks need to go into hibernation. If you’re planning to escape the cold for somewhere sunny this winter, a good pair should be in your suitcase. The beauty of men’s swim trunks is that they can be worn in or out of the water, doubling as the ultimate beachside bottoms or everyday shorts. The best swim trunks for men today have a moisture-wicking and quick-drying fabric, four-way stretch for mobility, a flattering length, and an athletic fit. Finding the right one for you can be a challenge, which is why we're here to help. Our team of fashion editors spent the past year trying and testing swim trunks to find options that blend comfort and style.

Over the past four years, I’ve tested more than 20 different pairs of swim trunks—everything from legacy surf brands to buzzy newcomers—but Fair Harbor’s have consistently exceeded my expectations. This pair nails that trifecta of being stylish, functional, and worth the price.

The first thing I noticed: the fabric. It’s a cotton-poly blend that feels smooth and broken-in right out of the gate. It doesn’t feel like any of that stiff, swishy, overly synthetic feel you get with most swim trunks. I’m usually quick to write off built-in liners altogether, but the BreezeKnit liner changed my mind. It feels more like a supportive pair of boxer briefs than the usual scratchy mesh. It’s snug (but comfortable on the crown jewels), breathable, and, most importantly, it doesn’t ride up or chafe. I’ve worn it for full beach days in Puerto Rico—swimming, walking, grabbing lunch—and never once felt the need to adjust.

The 7-inch inseam hits just above the knee on me, giving it a clean, tailored look. It’s an easy middle ground that works whether you’re getting in the water or just wearing it as your default summer short. There’s enough stretch in the cotton-polyester fabric that I never feel restricted. Plus, it comes in seersucker versions, solid-colored options, and other unique patterns. The hidden zipper pocket stashes a key or card without them slipping out, and the side pockets don’t balloon up in the water—something a lot of trunks still get wrong. It’s not a substitute for a gym short, but the fabric dries quickly for other oceanside activities.

I can’t get enough of the R&R Trunk's timeless style, functional fabric, and flattering fit. I love the no-fuss design with a tailored cut that’s not too baggy or slim. Coupled with the flexible waistband, the fit looks great on most body types. It’s available in two inseams–5.5 and 7.5 inches. The latter provides enough coverage and hits a couple inches above the knee for most men (our universal style recommendation for shorts). Though I wore the shorter length on the beach during my stay in Miami because it shows off my summer leg gains.

Rhone’s athleisure performs just as well as it looks. I’ve sweat-tested the R&R during beachside runs and volleyball games, and found that its odor-fighting fabric kept me feeling fresh. The mesh liner kept my family jewels locked in, without cutting off circulation. A few editors on our style team who have the R&R trunk say that the liner really does have a second-skin like quality. That’s probably because the polyester blend fabric is stretchy, which felt more comfortable than Lululemon’s (also great!) Swim Short. These durable features also mean the R&R Trunk doubles as a decent gym short if you’re in a pinch, and saves you one less thing to pack for a tropical vacation. We love that it comes in 11 colorways, but if you want to go classic, you can’t go wrong with the Electric Blue or Navy option.

The absence of liner offers a comfortable commando style, which is why I prefer a pair like this one from Lululemon. I don’t have to be bothered with any mesh material that feels restrictive or scratchy against my crown jewels—I can just slip it on and head into the water. I also love that the minimal design doesn’t scream “swim trunk”, so I can go from brunch to the boardwalk or the pool without having to do an outfit change. It passes as an everyday short, which is exactly the kind of versatility I want in the summer. The polyester-elastomultiester fabric has so much stretch, it performs just as good—if not better—than most of my gym shorts.

I’ve worn this pair for pickup volleyball and quick workouts, and they move with you instead of clinging or sagging out. It also dries fast and doesn't get that heavy, waterlogged feel after a swim, which makes a huge difference if you’re posted up poolside for a while. The 7-inch inseam is short enough to show some quad, but long enough that it still feels put-together if you’re grabbing a drink after. On my 5’8” frame, it lands a couple inches above the knee with a clean, tailored look—not too baggy, not too slim. If you’re taller, it’ll read a bit shorter and sportier; shorter guys get that ideal mid-thigh cut without going full retro.

After testing Proof’s Performance Swim Trunk, we found that it’s easily the most durable short on this list. Our editors appreciate the polyester-spandex blend fabric, which is stretchy, quick drying, and nearly tear proof. We’ve sported this during tropical hikes and extreme water sports, and found that the Performance Trunk held up to just about anything mother nature threw at it. We like the moisture-wicking liner, which is actually more comfortable than Rhone’s R&R short, but we did find it didn’t dry as quickly as Rhone’s short, and is a bit thicker than we’d prefer. Still, those are minor quibbles for a swim trunk as functional as this one.

Looks-wise, the Performance Trunk isn’t the most stylish of the bunch, and it’s not meant to be. It’s available in six solid colors and two inseam options, all of which have a no-frills design. Though we have to say, because of its barebones aesthetics, the Performance Trunk looks a lot cleaner than your typical bulky hiking short. Proof markets this as a multipurpose trunk that doubles as a gym short, and after putting it through the paces, we agree with that claim. While it’s not as breathable as Ten Thousand’s award-winning Interval Short, Proof’s stretchy fabric moves easily through all sorts of workouts.

For your next vacation, you need a dressy swim trunk that can look great at the beach, bar, or restaurant. Enter this one from Bather, which has a plaid-like pattern with complementing tones of maroon and blue. This makes it more polished than your typical swim shorts, so you can easily pair it with a simple polo or the brand’s matching camp shirt and sandals for a foolproof, lunchtime fit in your arsenal. I’ve worn it to a five-star hotel’s restaurant and then straight to the pool for a mid-day cocktail.

The waistband rests gently on the waist, but you can adjust the fit using the drawstrings. Unlike the scratchy net-like liners in cheaper swim trunks, the nylon-spandex blend is silky and irritation-free, so I could wear it for hours and be comfortable. Plus, the 5.5-inch inseam flatters tall and short guys alike. In terms of functionality, the pockets are super deep for your sunglasses or wallet, while one in the back snaps shut for extra security.

Fair Harbor offers so many great trunks, we couldn't help but to feature the Anchor Short, too. It's available in a variety of solids and prints, but we're big fans of the red stripe option, since it has a cool ‘80s vibe that pairs well with laidback T-shirts, tank tops, and more. This style also comes with the BreezeKnit liner—Fair Harbor's soft, supportive alternative to traditional mesh liner found in swimwear. It provides a snug and comfortable feel, while keeping you cool as ice.

Unlike other picks on this list, The Anchor Trunk is available in three inseams. The 6-inch inseam is great for guys who want to show off their hard-earned leg gains this summer. The 8-inch inseam hits the sweet spot between casual and polished, a safe bet if you're unsure which to go for. And the 10-inch inseam is the longest option, ideal for those who prefer a bit more coverage. Plus, its relaxed (not baggy) fit keeps this from veering into Reno 911! territory.

Ralph Lauren’s classic style is the most versatile of the bunch—it works as a swim trunk, a casual short, and even a workout short. I’ve worn it for early runs along the boardwalk, knocked out quick leg circuits on vacation, and then jumped straight into the water without needing to change. The 5.75-inch inseam gives it a shorter, more athletic cut that feels mobile and unrestrictive, especially when you’re moving. But its trimmer, more style-forward look makes it clean enough to pass as an everyday short.

It’s made from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries quickly and has just enough stretch that you can bend down or twist at any turn. The mesh liner feels breathable and supportive, unlike traditional swim trunks. And because the silhouette is sleek and the design is minimal—save for that signature embroidered pony—it pairs easily with a tee or button-down, making it a true wear-all-day option for beach trips, resort hangs, or any summer day that doesn’t stick to one lane.

Sure, this is the most expensive option on our list, but we think Orlebar Brown's Bulldog Trunk packs serious style that’s worthy of its higher price point. The polyester-elastane fabric is designed with a textured stripe pattern, which is very sharp and unexpected—something most guys would shy away from, so you’ll probably be the only guy at the pool rocking it. I wore mine to the beach in Costa Rica, and no one had anything remotely close to this pair; only baggy boardshort-like types.

This one lands mid-thigh at a 6-inch inseam, which is the golden length for most men. It’s not as stretchy as the Rhone pair, but you’re not rocking this for comfort; the Bulldog is all about quiet luxury. When I’m not in the water, I wear it with just about any solid polo or camp shirt for a five-star resort fit. Plus, the gold fasteners on the waist add extra style points, and just look super plush.

If you’re looking for something more surf-specific, the California-based brand best known for its laid-back, surfer aesthetic delivers the Cruise Boardshort. It’s cut from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries impressively fast, making it ideal for long days in and out of the water. The scalloped leg—where the hem curves slightly upward at the outer thigh—gives you a greater range of motion and a subtle retro-sport look. It’s one of those design tweaks that looks cool but also improves mobility.

It’s built to stay put. The double drawcord waistband adds extra security, so even when you’re getting knocked around by waves or caught in a strong current, you’re not worrying about your trunks slipping. It’s a small but clutch feature if you’re actually swimming, surfing, or doing anything more active than lounging.

Patagonia used a creative, cloudy effect across its lengthy boardshort that looks like sun-faded tie-dye you’d find on a well-traveled surf trip. It’s stylish enough to stand out amongst a sea of guys in basic trunks. Like Vuori’s option, this pair falls right above the knee, providing more coverage in case your shorts ride up as you get out of the water. I’m 5'8" and the 18-inch outseam fits pretty long on me, so the fit is more flattering for taller guys around 6’ feet. If you want things even longer, the brand also offers a 21-inch version that hovers over the knee.

Despite the trimmer leg, the cut never feels restrictive—it’s got enough room to move without baggy. It’s made with a lightweight polyester-spandex fabric that has a slightly sturdier structure than most of the swim trunks, but flexes whether you’re paddling out or diving a volleyball. I found it dries down quickly between dips, and the double looped waistband ensures it stays secure.

Patagonia’s Baggies Short has proven its durability on everything from multi-day hikes to back-to-back swimming sessions. Our guys have worn this trunk for backpacking through rugged trails, jumping into rivers, and air-drying in the sun—day after day—without wearing them out. The tough nylon fabric resists abrasion from rocks, sand, and saltwater, while the water-repellent coating helps it dry quickly.

Unlike traditional slanted pockets that can balloon up in the water, this pair has mesh openings inside, so the water flows out and doesn’t weigh you down. Despite dozens of uses and hours in the ocean, we haven’t seen these trunks fade, fray, or lose shape. Our fashion editors found they pair nicely with a string of T-shirts and sneakers for coffee pick-ups or quick grocery runs.

Sometimes, swim trunks with loud designs can be too in-your-face, but Mack Weldon went easy on this pair. It’s decked out with a dotted gradient pattern that adds a visual pop, without looking tacky. Our editors have worn this with a white polo to balance things out, and works as a foolproof fit for beachside lunches. We especially like the fit: it’s relaxed, but slimmer than the Bather swim trunks for a dressier vibe.

Like most of the swim trunks on this list, this version is made with a polyester-spandex flex that offers a lot of mobility. We could maintain a full range of motion through running, squatting and walking. During our testing, the mesh liner didn’t irritate our family jewels either. In fact, it was one of the more comfortable liners on the list.

If you're performing heavy activities in swimsuits, consider doing without liners. Board shorts, for instance, aren't made with liners for more wiggle room and comfort. Otherwise, liners should fit snugly, but should never be too tight or pinch your skin. Built-in mesh liners provide extra support to your down-there and keep everything in place as you move. Since they're mesh, they're also breathable and quick-drying.

Shorts are getting shorter, and so are swim trunks. But you don't have to chase trends. Typically, around 7 inches in inseam length is a universally flattering fit that hits a couple inches above the thigh. Though if you want to show off your quads, you can't go wrong with a 5-inch inseam, either. If you're looking at outseam lengths, 14-inch is more fashion-forward, 17-inch is a casual mid-length, and 20-inch is as full coverage as you can get without wearing pants.

If you're swimming, surfing, or just moving around a lot in bathing suits, Stafford advises stretch as a must-have factor, since it allows a great fit and range of motion in and out of the water.

Waistbands should fit comfortably on your body, and a drawstring may help you to adjust the waist size if needed. We recommend a full-elastic waistband with a drawcord because it ensures you keep your trunks on, even if you’re diving from the high dive. If you’re going for a snap closure, just make sure it’s not too tight with the ability to unsnap after one beer.

To find the best swim trunks for men, our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, spent the past five years testing more than 100 swim trunks in a variety of settings. For instance, we went whitewater rafting in Proof's performance shorts, swam laps in Rhone's R&R short, and sported Orlebar Brown swim trunks at the beach. From there, we evaluated these swim trunks based on their style, fit, price point, performance in and out of the water, and versatility to make the final top picks.

Bonus points if they doubled as athletic shorts or hiking shorts. Specifically, we looked for styles that are not trendy or trend-chasing; instead, our picks of the best swim trunks have a flattering fit, provide a ton of value at reasonable price points, and come in styles that will look great years from now.

The 12 best swim trunks for men tested by our style editors below are all quick-drying, comfortable, and look great. Whether you're planning to wear these to the beach, poolside, or to your weekend lunch, the best swim trunks for men have you covered.

Obviously, cotton is a no-go—it gets way too heavy when met with water. Our fashion team recommends lightweight synthetic fabrics since they dry quickly and are usually fade-resistant to the sun and chlorine. These synthetic fabrics are ideal for underwater wear because they won't get hefty and pull you down when drenched in water.

Poly with the addition of stretch (Lycra, elastane) material is the most common with good reason—more comfortable, forgiving. Some brands use nylon instead of poly because it absorbs less water and does not get heavy as the waterproofing wears off over time, but nylon does not (take color) dye as deeply and vibrantly as poly.

Choosing the right color and print for men's swim trunks boils down to personal style, skin tone, body type, and occasion. If you prefer a more classic and versatile look, solid colors like navy, blue, or olive are excellent choices that can easily transition from the beach to casual outings. If you want something a bit more eye-catching, subtle patterns like stripes or small geometric prints add personality without being too loud. For those who like to stand out, bright colors, tropical florals, or retro-inspired prints make a strong statement, especially on an island.

Your skin tone can also guide your choice—fairer skin tones tend to work best with earth tones and pastels, while medium to tan skin pairs well with rich blues, corals, or reds. Darker tones can pull off almost any color, but bright neons and strong contrasts pop especially well. Body type plays a factor too—shorter guys might benefit from vertical stripes or a shorter inseam to create a lengthening effect, while taller guys can balance their frame with medium-to-long inseams and bold patterns. Athletic builds look great in solid colors and tailored fits that highlight their shape, whereas stockier builds might find that darker shades or micro-prints create a more streamlined look.

Lastly, think about where you'll be wearing swim trunks. For pool parties and resort vacations, playful prints and vibrant hues add to the fun, while sporty designs with color-blocking work well for active beach days. If you're looking for swim trunks that can double as everyday shorts, muted tones or subtle patterns offer the most versatility. Ultimately, the best choice is whatever makes you feel confident and comfortable.

#5067. DOJ Targets 800 Defendants in Largest-Ever Scam Crackdown, Including Crypto Fraud

The U.S. Justice Department said Tuesday that its largest-ever crackdown on scammers has produced actions against more than 800 defendants since March, with cryptocurrency investment fraud run out of Southeast Asian scam centers among its top targets.

The department announced the results of an anti-scam surge that followed President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14390, signed March 6. Since then, prosecutors have acted in more than 400 cases, bringing new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts and sentences across 85 federal districts.

U.S. agents also helped police in more than 10 countries raid foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans. Thirty defendants were extradited to face charges in U.S. courts.

“Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning.”

Crypto sits at the center of much of the effort. The State Department said the U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement it funds and trains have helped freeze more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts.

The Justice Department’s Scam Center Strike Force, formed in 2025 to go after Southeast Asian crypto fraud, says its crypto seizure team has restrained about $1.08 billion in cryptocurrency from these schemes. The team is focused on returning stolen funds to victims.

The FBI’s Operation Blackout has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices and helped dismantle more than 29 scam compounds across Asia, Africa and the Middle East, the department said. The FBI also helped free and repatriate more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to run scams inside those compounds.

“The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you,” FBI Director Kash Patel said.

In the past month alone, the Criminal Division filed or unsealed charges against more than 30 scam defendants, including those tied to Southeast Asian scam centers running crypto investment fraud schemes. Other cases involved inheritance fraud, jury duty imposters working from Georgia prisons and sweepstakes schemes aimed at elderly Americans.

The Secret Service said it has restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds during the surge. One of its cases identified a crypto investment conspiracy run from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in California over his alleged role.

In Moldova, State Department-backed raids in October shut down five call centers and led to the detention of eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake crypto trading platforms. The SEC said that in the last year it charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million.

Homeland Security Investigations said its fraud cases have led to the seizure or freezing of more than $120 million, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts.

The crackdown builds on months of pressure on overseas fraud rings. Trump planned to highlight the push against overseas crypto scams in October, and the U.S. government seized more than $580 million in crypto linked to Southeast Asian scam networks in February. In October 2025, prosecutors moved to seize 127,271 bitcoin tied to a Southeast Asian scam operation.

The stakes are large. Citing Gallup, the department said 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, directly or through someone in their household, and Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025, including crypto investment scams.

The department noted that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

#5066. Bought Nvidia stock during the 2017 crypto boom? You could qualify for a $290 million settlement

Eligible Nvidia investors who bought shares during the 2017–2018 crypto mining boom could share in a $290 million settlement.

Investors who bought or otherwise acquired Nvidia common stock from Aug. 10, 2017, through Nov. 15, 2018, could share in a proposed $290 million cash settlement if the court approves the deal and their claims qualify.

The parties filed the agreement on Nov. 24, and plaintiffs filed an unopposed motion for preliminary approval that day in federal court in Oakland.

The plaintiffs alleged that Nvidia and Jensen Huang misled investors about how much crypto miners contributed to sales of graphics chips Nvidia marketed for gaming.

They say shareholders suffered losses after the extent of Nvidia’s mining exposure emerged in 2018. Nvidia and Huang deny wrongdoing, and the settlement agreement contains no admission of liability.

The court certified the class in March, covering individuals and entities. Exclusions include the defendants, Nvidia officers and directors at relevant times, certain relatives and related entities, and the defendants’ liability insurers. Investors whose requests to opt out are accepted by the court are also excluded.

Class members seeking payment would have to file a paper or electronic claim by a court-set deadline, with documents supporting their claimed loss.

Under the proposed allocation, approved claimants would share the net fund in proportion to the losses the plan recognizes for their stock transactions.

The plan would use the investor’s documented transactions, including what they paid for the shares and what they received if they sold them, but the court would have to approve the allocation plan.

The net fund would include the cash settlement and accrued interest, less taxes, notice and administration costs, court-awarded legal fees and litigation expenses, and other court-approved costs.

Individual payments would depend on the amount left in the fund and the total recognized losses from approved claims.

The parties accepted a mediator’s recommendation on Sept. 24 and notified the court of their agreement on Oct. 22.

The public docket lists Feb. 4, 2027, at 2 p.m. for the preliminary-approval hearing before Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. in Oakland.

If he grants preliminary approval, the proposed schedule calls for postcard notices to start going out and the claim form to be posted within 20 calendar days of the order. Claims would be due 90 calendar days after the notice date.
