#5062. The 11 Best War Movies About Brotherhood, Ranked

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Ahead of Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl, we’ve pulled together a list of gripping films that show how bonds between men survive—and sometimes break—under fire.

DIRECTOR PETER BERG had never made a World War II movie before The Mosquito Bowl, but he certainly knows a thing or two about football. The director of Friday Night Lights has returned to a world of cocksure young players with their whole lives ahead of them in dire need of rousing their morale—only now it’s the true story of the football game between two World War II Marine regiments at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944. There’s another connection: both The Mosquito Bowl and Friday Night Lights are adapted from books by author Buzz Bissinger.

Berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service. After enduring years of the Pacific campaign, they realize how valuable the team spirit and camaraderie of football can be as the Battle of Okinawa looms ahead of them.

The Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood. The deeply felt connection between soldiers is the lifeblood of historical war films; when done convincingly, a squad’s well-earned devotion and loyalty add rich melodrama to the action. Brotherhood is just as compelling when it is subverted—like the respect felt between soldiers on opposing sides, or when hardened, broken combatants struggle to express the empathy and compassion they feel. The best war movies know that brotherhood endures after the fighting stops, but in different forms—softer, stranger, when it’s hard to reconcile the memories of war with a world that continues as normal.

To mark the Thanksgiving release of The Mosquito Bowl on Netflix, we ranked the most gripping and rousing war films about brotherhood.

An ensemble of actors you'd typically see in a "Young Stars of Tomorrow" profile immerse themselves in a U.S. Navy SEAL platoon and recreate a real-time Iraq War firefight that co-director Ray Mendoza was a part of. Opening with the platoon jubilantly dancing to "Call On Me" streamed through their base's crappy internet, Warfare quickly adopts a stripped-back and meticulous play-by-play of how one slice of warfare was actually experienced. You get a sense of brotherhood from the practiced, reflexive interactions between SEALs, and their interdependence also helped build the film, as Mendoza and co-director Alex Garland drew from the testimonies of his fellow soldiers when writing the script. The stylistic choices—like a thundering sound mix and infrequent use of satellite photography—add an extra layer of tension to Warfare's depiction of courage under fire. It’s one of the most visceral movies in recent memory about modern war.

Before he brought us high-octane visions of robot cops and ambitious showgirls, Paul Verhoeven directed a handful of smash hits in his native Netherlands, including this Golden Globe-nominated war epic about the diverging fates of Dutch students during the Nazi occupation. Led by a supremely dashing Rutger Hauer, Soldier of Orange begins in 1938 and follows the wartime trajectory of Erik Lanshof, an initially neutral but increasingly principled aristocrat who protects his Dutch Resistance friends and distances himself from fascist collaborators. Before long, his entire school group has pledged one type of loyalty or another. Observed over a period of time, war reveals everything, and Erik’s blossoming heroism emerges as a result of his friendships all changing—for better or worse.

Forgive us for taking a creative approach to the headline so early in the list: Hell in the Pacific features no battles or squadron camaraderie, and takes place on a deserted island with only two characters—an American pilot (Lee Marvin) and a Japanese army captain (Toshiro Mifune)—who don’t understand a word the other person says. Even without comprehension, the American and Japanese soldiers find a hundred ways to rile each other up, including shock tactics, sabotage, pranks, and even makeshift imprisonment. Gradually, they realize each other’s company is the strongest connection to their starving humanity available to them, even if they’re affected in a way they can’t explain. Free from the rhetoric and politics of war, Marvin and Mifune play men who slip into a state of brash, stubborn childishness, and a brotherly kinship forms in spite of their inherent opposition.

Clint Eastwood and Steven Spielberg sound like an odd pair to collaborate on a war picture, but Eastwood’s pared-down, melancholic visual style is a terrific fit for this post-Band of Brothers war movie. Flags of Our Fathers wasn’t received as positively as its Japanese-language companion film Letters from Iwo Jima, but it’s a robust and affecting watch—splitting its runtime between the overwhelming Battle of Iwo Jima and its aftermath, where three soldiers celebrated as the iconic “flag-raisers” spent the final year of the Pacific Campaign on a spiritually draining propaganda tour. Flags of Our Fathers takes the essential themes of war cinema—brotherhood, sacrifice, heroism—and juxtaposes them with the United States military manufacturing their own national images and narratives in real time. The tension between the brutal experience of being a brother-in-arms and the sanitized version promoted by war’s survivors makes for a powerful watch.

It’s as if director David Ayer (Suicide Squad, Bright) made a WWII movie to hammer home two points: tank warfare was a nightmare, and soldier hazing was way more hardcore than what you see in Band of Brothers. In the final months of the war in Europe, Wardaddy (Brad Pitt) rolls his bloody and battered tank unit slowly toward Berlin, and the arrival of fresh-faced pencil-pusher Norman (Logan Lerman) gives the hardened squad a chance to berate and bully the newcomer about all the ways he is soft, and war is hell. As their fellow brothers-in-arms are increasingly blasted apart into viscera, Wardaddy’s take-no-shit squad bolsters their unsentimental unity, and each of the five traumatized brothers rely on each other to watch their back and keep them sane on a frontline that might as well be the border to hell.

Spike Lee’s bracing film about the scars of Vietnam takes a familiar concept—a jaded band of veterans who try to pull off a heist—and spins it in a thorny, unpredictable direction. Four older Black veterans (led by an intense, captivating, and Oscar-snubbed Delroy Lindo) return to ‘Nam to recover the CIA gold their squadron hid during the war—aside from a delayed payday, it’s also the ultimate memorial of their late squad leader Norman (Chadwick Boseman). Marked by years of bitterness and PTSD, the “Bloods” retrace their steps while juggling painful reflections on how the war left them angry and guilty. When they're ambushed in the jungle and have to pick up guns again, we're reminded that Lee is never satisfied sticking in one narrative mode for too long, but the jagged catharsis of cranky, once-loyal soldiers confronting their wounds is far more visceral to watch.

When Private Alex (Harry Styles) says, “We're regimental brothers, mate,” in the belly of a fishing trawler on Dunkirk Beach, he’s not acting nobly—he’s making the case for throwing a soldier he thinks is German (he’s actually French) to the Nazis surrounding them. So much of Christopher Nolan’s war film about the perilous evacuation of Allied troops from France’s northernmost beaches centers on division: soldier feuds, breakdowns in communication, and a nonlinear narrative that takes place over a week or an hour depending on who’s in front of the camera. But Dunkirk’s staggering disaster and survival action builds to an overwhelming climactic sense of unity. Across every mini-arc and timeline, Nolan shows us countless pairs of soldiers, pilots, and civilians who stand together as symbolic brothers.

After the famously gnarly and disorienting D-Day beach landing sequence—which has influenced every WWII action movie since, including The Mosquito Bowl—Saving Private Ryan settles into the most iconic band of brothers story outside of… well, Band of Brothers, co-created by this film’s director and star. Tom Hanks is the grouchy uncle leading a reluctant squad to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (Matt Damon) from the front lines after his brothers were killed in action. The squadron's trudge through France is fueled with banter, grumbling, and the type of resentment that stews between siblings who hate when someone receives special treatment. Steven Spielberg’s gift for balancing movie-star gravitas and off-the-cuff charisma is on full display in the ensemble, but no gruff, hot-tempered soldier has a response to Private Ryan's justification for not returning to his mom: “Tell her that when you found me, I was here, and I was with the only brothers I have left.”

The only war film on this list to be set before the 20th century and at sea, the Napoleonic Wars-era Master and Commander has a reputation for being a “dudes/gentlemen rock” classic: the reputation still holds up. Under the command of Captain Jack Aubrey (Russell Crowe), the HMS Surprise wages war against a French frigate that taunts the crew across the seas. Majestic naval battles aside, much of Master and Commander has a warm hangout tone, focusing on the kinship between Aubrey and ship’s surgeon Maturin, their interest in classical music and botanical science, and revelrous suppers in the captain’s quarters. It's impossible to watch Peter Weir’s sea epic and not pine for the brotherly loyalty (maybe not the seasickness or cannonball attacks) that Aubrey inspires here. Nothing will make you feel the romantic thrill of adventure like Master and Commander.

Pick your favorite scene from The Deer Hunter: the riotous wedding party, the spontaneous Frankie Valli singalong over a game of pool, or the exacting game of Russian roulette played by prisoners of war. They each shine a light on the ordinary, working-class brotherhood that was completely transformed by the Vietnam War. This Oscar-winning epic builds complex, traumatized characters (played by Robert De Niro, John Cazale, and Christopher Walken) who reckon with never being able to experience their relationships and community in the same way again. The Deer Hunter paints such a disturbing and fragile picture of the “before and after” of Vietnam, as each brotherly bond becomes charged with alienation and despair. Notorious for its multiple “death game” sequences, The Deer Hunter excels in making its harrowing portrayal of war and PTSD genuinely heartbreaking.

One of the best things to come out of legendary Hong Kong filmmakers John Woo and Tsui Hark falling out was the future director of Hard Boiled and Face/Off leaving the iconic A Better Tomorrow series to make this searing war story. Beginning in the late ’60s, it focuses on three close friends (Tony Leung, Jacky Cheung, Waise Lee) whose smuggling ambitions dunk them headfirst in the brutality and desperation of the Vietnam War. Bullet in the Head blends the epic sweep of New Hollywood war epics (Apocalypse Now, The Deer Hunter) with Woo’s “heroic bloodshed” toolkit, which meant electric action spectacle and bold, tragic melodrama. An underrated operatic beast in Woo’s stacked filmography—not to mention a personal one, as Woo used the film to express his reaction to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre—the action is always in service of a high-stakes tri-friendship that can only take so much passion and betrayal before the treasured brotherhood breaks.

Rory Doherty is a critic and journalist based in Edinburgh, Scotland. His work can be found at British GQ, Vulture, Inverse, AV Club, and other publications. He can be found on Twitter/X at @roryhasopinions

#5061. Bithumb Says October Hack Exposed Passports, Bank Accounts and Wallet Addresses

South Korean crypto exchange Bithumb said Wednesday that an October hack of its internal systems exposed more people and far more personal data than it first disclosed, including passport numbers, bank account numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

The exchange also said the intruder had access for about 15 days before being shut out, not the roughly one hour it reported last month.

In an updated notice posted Nov. 25, Bithumb said a follow-up review of the breach of Daou Office, its internal mobile groupware system, turned up additional affected people and additional types of data. The company said the new findings stem from the same incident it disclosed on Oct. 29.

Bithumb now says an unauthorized outside party accessed the groupware system from 1:49 p.m. on Oct. 12 to 3:22 p.m. on Oct. 27, Korea time, and took personal information and files stored there.

That is a sharp change from its first account. Bithumb had said the hack lasted about an hour, from 11:28 a.m. to 12:27 p.m. on Oct. 27, and that it detected the intrusion at 12:14 p.m. that day. The revised timeline means the attacker went unnoticed for more than two weeks.

Bithumb first reported that the data of 6,444 customers and 715 employees, or 7,159 people in total, had been exposed. It did not give an updated count on Wednesday. The notice lists customers, employees of partner companies and current and former staff among those affected.

The list of exposed data now runs to 19 items. It includes member numbers, names, mobile numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, resident registration numbers, passport numbers and driver’s license numbers.

It also covers bank account numbers, home addresses, gender, nationality, copies of ID documents, occupations, employer names and work contact details, as well as transaction histories and wallet addresses. Bithumb said not every item applies to every person, and that affected users will be told individually by email and text message what was taken.

For crypto users, the wallet addresses and transaction records stand out. Paired with names and phone numbers, that kind of data can help scammers target people they know hold digital assets.

Bithumb said Daou Office is an internal business system separate from customer exchange accounts and asset data. It said it has found no sign that its exchange service systems or customer database were directly breached, and that it has stepped up real-time monitoring of unusual trades and withdrawals.

The exchange said it blocked the attacker’s IP addresses, fixed the vulnerability behind the incident and is running a security review of all of its externally exposed services. It has also set up a dedicated support desk for victims that covers financial and legal counseling as well as compensation reviews.

“We will take responsibility for all harm confirmed to have resulted from this personal information breach and provide all necessary support and compensation to affected customers,” Bithumb said.

Bithumb warned users that it never asks for passwords, verification codes or OTP details by phone, text or messenger. It urged anyone who gets such a request to stop responding, confirm through its official app or customer center and report any financial losses to police.

The disclosure adds to a difficult year for the exchange. Bithumb mistakenly credited users with billions of dollars in bitcoin in February, and regulators fined it $24 million and imposed a six-month partial suspension in March over anti-money laundering violations.

It also comes as South Korea weighs new rules for crypto exchanges, including a 20% cap on ownership stakes. Brokerages including Mirae Asset Securities and Daishin Securities have also suffered a series of cyberattacks.

“We are thoroughly investigating the cause of the incident,” Bithumb said.

#5060. USDT leads borrowing on four of six DeFi protocols examined by Europe’s banking watchdog

The EBA urges the EU to assess restrictions on crypto firms facilitating loans involving USDT and other unauthorized stablecoins.

Tether’s USDT led stablecoin borrowing on Aave, Fluid and Spark in a July 30 snapshot published by the European Banking Authority (EBA) on Nov. 25.

The EBA renewed its call for the European Commission to assess rules for firms that give customers access to decentralized lending, including possible restrictions on loans involving stablecoins that lack the required EU authorization.

In its comparison of six lending protocols, the regulator grouped USDT and its USDT0 bridged version when describing demand on Aave, Fluid and Spark. The EBA also found that borrowers on JustLend overwhelmingly favored USDT and pointed to the token’s dominance on the Tron blockchain.

USDC accounted for a larger share of active loans than USDT on Compound and Morpho.

The EBA measured each stablecoin against all active loans on the same protocol. Separate estimates suggest EU participation in decentralized finance remains limited, and self-hosted wallets and reporting gaps make it difficult to identify where users are based.

The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) requires authorization for covered stablecoins to be offered to the public or admitted to trading in the EU, and USDT lacks that authorization.

The EBA’s summary of MiCA’s scope says fully decentralized services operating without an intermediary fall outside the rules. The report says some EU consumers may hold stablecoins like USDT in wallets they control themselves.

#5055. Switzerland Picks 57 Countries for Crypto Tax Data Sharing Starting in 2028

Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 countries and territories with which the country plans to automatically share tax information on crypto users starting in 2028, extending its long-standing bank data exchange to bitcoin and other digital assets.

The list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and various G20 countries, the State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) said in a release on Wednesday. The exchange will run under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, known as CARF.

With the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release. The government did not name the 57 jurisdictions beyond those broad groups, and it did not publish the full list alongside the announcement.

Data will not flow to every name on the list. An exchange will take place only if a partner jurisdiction wants to swap information with Switzerland and meets the conditions of the OECD standard, in particular its requirements on confidentiality and data security.

Before any financial account or crypto data changes hands, the Federal Council will run a targeted check of whether each partner complies with OECD standards. It will rely on a review mechanism Parliament approved on Sept. 28, 2026, which covers both the older exchange of bank account data and the new crypto exchange.

The domestic legal basis for the crypto exchange took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. Earlier this month, though, the SIF said the framework could not be implemented before Jan. 1, 2027, because the partner list still needed approval and notifications had to go to the OECD. The rules do not apply this year.

The Council also approved Armenia and Rwanda as new partners for the exchange of financial account information, with first exchanges due in 2028, and signed off on two notifications needed to carry out the exchange. Both partner lists were broadly supported during public consultations in 2024 and 2025, the government said.

The final list is shorter than first planned. In June 2025, the Federal Council proposed 74 countries relevant to the crypto market, including all EU states, the UK and most G20 members. That plan left out the United States and Saudi Arabia, and it targeted a 2026 start with first data exchanges in 2027.

Wednesday’s release did not say which countries were dropped or whether the U.S. is now on the list. The U.S. has committed to begin CARF exchanges by 2029, according to the OECD’s Global Forum, which lists Switzerland among 27 jurisdictions aiming for first exchanges by 2028.

That U.S. timeline is already shaping policy elsewhere. South Korea pushed its 22% crypto tax back to 2029 partly because it will not receive American crypto trading data until CARF exchanges with the U.S. begin that year. Officials said taxing earlier could put Korea’s domestic market at a disadvantage.

Switzerland’s decision lands as European governments debate how much they should know about crypto holders. On Tuesday, France’s Senate rejected a rule that would have forced bitcoin holders to declare self-custody wallets, while EU states began collecting crypto transaction data under the bloc’s DAC8 directive this year.

For Switzerland, CARF extends a system it already runs for bank accounts. The country has exchanged financial account information automatically under the OECD’s Common Reporting Standard since 2018, ending much of the secrecy once tied to Swiss banking. Its regulated crypto market keeps growing, with the country’s financial regulator clearing its first bitcoin ETF in October.

Under CARF, crypto service providers in Switzerland will have to collect information on users who are tax residents of activated partner jurisdictions and report it to Swiss tax authorities, which then pass it on to those partners once the exchange begins.

#5054. Ethereum’s quantum defense plans could delay a major upgrade to stop transaction censorship

Ethereum developers weigh how to deliver transaction censorship protections alongside work on quantum-resistant consensus.

Ethereum’s core developers kept a proposal to curb transaction censorship on the schedule for an upgrade called Hegotá at their Nov. 26 meeting.

They deferred a final decision while client teams considered whether the work could run alongside efforts to make the network’s consensus system resistant to quantum attacks.

The proposal, known as FOCIL, remains Hegotá’s lead consensus change. The All Core Devs call record puts the next review of the fork’s scope around Dec. 10.

Under draft EIP-7805, a committee of validators would broadcast lists of transactions waiting in the public queue. Validators that vote on the next block would check the lists they received before a cutoff.

If a builder leaves out a listed transaction that is still valid at the end of the block and fits in the remaining gas, those validators would withhold their votes. They would ignore lists from a committee member they saw send conflicting versions.

For someone whose eligible transaction makes a timely list, a builder’s decision to leave it out could cost that block its votes.

EthPandaOps’ October Heze devnet plan carried forward tests of list propagation, timing, and how inclusion lists interact with the separation of block builders and proposers.

The team kept Frame Transactions, another Hegotá proposal, on a separate test track. The proposed Bogotá devnet would focus on execution-layer testing while teams wait for a decision before running a combined test.

FOCIL co-author Jihoon Song argues that developers and testers can move inclusion lists toward release while researchers work on post-quantum decoupled consensus, a redesign of how Ethereum agrees on blocks.

He would start with preregistration so validators can register new keys ahead of a switch in how they sign. Song expects most FOCIL work to be done by the time the consensus design is ready for client teams to implement for mainnet.

At the Nov. 24 post-quantum breakout, developers discussed how to restore a test network that stalled after some clients took too long to generate new validator keys. The test is part of the early consensus work the Ethereum Foundation described in its Nov. 23 update.

Ethlabs researcher Caspar Schwarz-Schilling argues that a small group of researchers and client developers with a broad view of Ethereum would be needed to deliver both changes safely.

He favors deferring FOCIL so that group can focus on consensus. The extent of the overlap depends in part on what developers expect the first version of FOCIL to handle.

Two proposals discussed on Nov. 26 would put FOCIL at different points in Ethereum’s transition to quantum-safe consensus.

The timing decision affects how soon eligible public transactions could gain stronger protection against being left out.

The paths show proposed sequencing. They convey no duration, staffing commitment or final fork decision.

The diagram maps proposals made on Nov. 26 and the shared integration questions described in the draft inclusion-list specification and Song’s compatibility analysis.

The paths show proposed sequencing. They convey no duration, staffing commitment or final fork decision.

The FOCIL draft relies on BLS signatures to authenticate the lists themselves, and those signatures would eventually need a quantum-resistant replacement.

In a separate technical analysis, Song also identifies work on how lists would carry larger post-quantum transactions or the proofs that could accompany them without overloading the network.

The decoupled consensus design also leaves open which group of validators would enforce the lists.

Barnabas Busa proposed a narrower version that would enforce inclusion for certain existing transaction types and excuse builders from including Frame Transactions.

Inclusion lists could then protect users of those existing transaction types in Hegotá, while users of Frame Transactions would have to wait for enforcement to cover them.

The next post-quantum consensus session is scheduled for Nov. 27 at 14:00 UTC. When developers return to Hegotá’s scope, the practical test is how much work the first version needs from the people designing the new consensus system.

#5048. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve Bill Clears House Committee, Heads to Floor

A bill that would write the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday.

The American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R. 8957, was filed with amendments as House Report 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789 on Nov. 24, according to congressional records. The committee had voted 28-21 to advance the bill at a Sept. 16 markup.

Rep. Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21. It now lists 23 cosponsors, including Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat, with Reps. Byron Donalds and Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida added on Nov. 24.

The reported text directs the Treasury secretary to set up a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile within 180 days of the law taking effect. Bitcoin owned by the federal government would move into the reserve, while other digital assets would go to the stockpile.

The centerpiece is a lock-up. Treasury would have to hold all bitcoin deposited in the reserve for at least 20 years after enactment, and during that period no reserve bitcoin could be “sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose.”

After the 20 years, the Treasury secretary could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve in any two-year period. Two years before the holding period ends, Treasury would have to send Congress recommendations on whether to keep holding or begin a gradual release.

Federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to give Treasury a full accounting of the bitcoin and other digital assets they hold or have seized. Until the reserve is set up, agencies could not sell those coins except for national security, when required by law or a court, or to return assets to crime victims.

The bill also creates a Proof of Reserve system. Treasury would publish an annual report on total holdings, transactions and control of private keys, checked by an independent auditor with expertise in cryptographic attestations, while the Government Accountability Office would provide oversight.

States could choose to store their own bitcoin in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, keeping title to the coins and the right to withdraw them.

The committee rewrote the bill before reporting it. Begich’s introduced text asked Treasury and Commerce to study funding bitcoin purchases with surplus remittances from Federal Reserve Banks or a revaluation of the Fed’s gold certificates, as well as with tax payments, tariff revenue and gifts.

Those options are gone from the amended study, which now looks at swapping other digital assets in the stockpile, forfeitures and settlements, and partnerships with states or private entities. The amended version also states that nothing in the study authorizes borrowing, pledging government assets as collateral, new taxes or deficit spending to buy bitcoin.

The committee also amended the bill’s title to drop a reference to offsetting costs with Federal Reserve resources, and removed a section that would have required the Exchange Stabilization Fund to report its bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin Magazine reported on the bill’s bipartisan debut in May and on the full text revealing the 20-year lock-up in June. The reserve itself already exists under Executive Order 14233, signed in March 2025, but an executive order can be reversed by a future president, which is why Begich and his cosponsors want it in statute.

Setting up the reserve has been slow. In July, a report said Treasury and Commerce were competing over who would control it.

Begich’s bill has not received a floor vote. If it passes the House, the Senate would still need to act before it could reach the president’s desk.

#5046. The 5 Best Laser Hair Growth Devices for Men in 2026, According to Doctors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

You don’t need to fly overseas to regrow hair.

THERE COMES A time in every man’s life—sans the few genetically gifted—when he must face hair loss. It hits sooner than many expect, as the American Hair Loss Association notes that 85 percent of men will face hair loss by age 50. There are then two options: lean into it and join the Stanley Tucci Gang, or invest in equipment to regrow hair. For the latter, the best tools to reverse balding at home are laser hair growth devices.

The majority of men lose their hair due to male pattern baldness (also known as androgenetic alopecia), a condition caused by genetic predisposition and hormonal influences, wherein testosterone is declining and dihydrotestosterone (aka DHT) is surging. This process is characterized by the classic receding hairline look, along with thinning around the crown.

Laser hair growth devices are best at treating this cause of hair loss, explains dermatologist and founder of Remedy, Dr. Muneeb Shah, MD. Other common factors like stress, illness, medications, nutritional deficiencies, and autoimmune diseases will be less responsive to laser therapies, as hair follicles are often damaged or inactive from these issues and less willing to be rebooted from light treatment.

Laser hair growth devices work by using low-level laser therapy, or LLLT, to stimulate weakened or dormant hair follicles, says hair restoration physician and creator of the Bauman Turbo LaserCap, Dr. Alan Bauman, MD. The process is known as photobiomodulation, and it involves exposing tissues to light in the red and near-infrared spectrum, which can improve cell metabolism and blood flow, reduce inflammation, and stimulate hair follicles to re-enter and maintain the growth phase.

Generally, LLLT does not include LED; instead, it uses laser diodes. However, some devices will combine both for added effectiveness or to reduce the intensity of laser diodes. “In simpler terms, laser therapy supercharges the environment for healthy hair growth by restoring energy to sluggish follicles and optimizing scalp conditions,” Dr. Bauman says.

Laser hair growth devices are rarely cheap (you won’t find an effective one below $400), so you want to make sure you’re getting the right option for you before making the investment. After chatting with the pros, these are the five laser hair growth devices worth considering.

The biggest dilemma when buying a laser hair growth device is choosing between LED and laser diodes, but with the iRestore Laser Therapy Hair Growth System, you don’t have to. This device uses a hybrid of laser diodes and LEDs to get the best of both worlds, pairing the gentle nature of LEDs with the power of laser diodes. Dr. Shah backs it, noting that iRestore is reputable and the device is FDA-cleared.

The brand even offers a six-month money-back guarantee if no results are seen. However, I’d imagine the brand doesn’t receive many sendbacks, as this device gives full coverage with serious results. That being said, Dr. Bauman warns that the combo of LED and laser diodes may dilute benefits for some due to mixed light sources. But hard to argue with a six-month guarantee.

Read More: iRestore Laser Face Mask Pro Review

Dr. Shah also recommends this offering from Current Body. This futuristic helmet offers a spectrum of red light LED from 620 to 660 nanometers. The flexible intensity allows for a customized experience, which is ideal for those new to these tools or with sensitive skin to ease into LED treatment and see what your ideal nanometer level is.

While results will be stronger closer to 650 or 660 nanometers, this range is powerful enough to reduce inflammation, decrease DHT levels (to maintain follicle strength), and improve blood flow on the scalp (to provide hair follicles with more oxygen and nutrients needed for growth).

Sure, it may look like a VR set from a scrapped Black Mirror episode, but it’s quite comfortable, and deceptively adjustable for a quality fit. Use for 10 minutes daily, and results can be seen quickly in as little as 16 weeks. The only reasons this helmet missed out on the top spot is that it relies solely on LED, and is roughly $300 more expensive than iRestore’s helmet.

Not everybody has the budget (or desire) to drop several thousand on a hair growth device. Maybe you’re on the fence about these tools, or the prospect of regrowing your hair in general. For these folks, Hairmax will be your best option, as it’s the least expensive tool on the market that’s still effective.

Featuring 12 medical-grade laser diodes in a comb-style tool, you gently brush this device through your hair and across your dome to stimulate hair growth. The sessions are listed at eight minutes; however, it often takes longer for the best results, given the manual nature of the device and the smaller surface it covers at once. Still, you won’t find a cheaper FDA-approved model.

Read More: Is Your Hair Loss From Thinning or Breaking

At first glance, the Hairmax LaserBand 82 looks like a nuisance to use. Rather than a cap design like HigherDose and Capillus, helmet like iRestore and Current Body, or Hairmax’s comb, the LaserBand resembles a mini MRI machine. But unlike those devices, this tool only needs to be used for a couple of minutes to see results, three times a week.

The brand boasts that sessions need only be 90 seconds, but Dr. Bauman warns it’ll take a bit longer for full coverage—like two or three minutes. Still, that’s by far the quickest treatment on this list. Plus, Dr. Bauman says it features a quality diode count (246 lasers), even if you may need to reposition after 90 seconds for full coverage.

Read More: Best Hair Thickening Shampoos for Men

Men’s Health writer Bob Gearing wore the HigherDose Red Light Therapy Hat every day for the past year, and swears by the results. He notes that this nifty cap is both more effective than Rogaine and less invasive, leaving no irritation or redness. It’s super easy to use, pop it on like any hat, and wear for 10 minutes a day while the 650 nanometer LED red light penetrates the scalp to promote a healthier environment for hair growth.

The brand lists 16 months as the target, but the best results will appear after six months. Unlike the Capillus cap, whose red light peaks through the sides during use, this is the only hair growth device you could get away with wearing in public without anyone noticing. It simply looks like a black hat, nothing more. This makes it both easy to use and even easier to incorporate into your daily routine.

As Dr. Bauman puts it, not all laser hair growth devices are created equal. The first thing to consider is what light is being used in your device to stimulate growth. The two primary options are LEDs (Light Emitting Diodes) and laser diodes. He recommends zeroing in on laser diodes as they’re more powerful and penetrate deeper into the scalp, targeting the hair follicle root more effectively.

From a strict regrowth perspective, laser diodes will be more effective; however, these also present more potential side effects given their strength, such as hyperpigmentation, burns, redness, and swelling. LEDs present fewer side effects, so they’re better for sensitive scalps, but they won’t penetrate the scalp and hair follicles as deeply. This means LED is best suited for early shedding and will struggle to help more severe hair loss.

For both LED and laser diode options, the therapeutic wavelength is crucial. Dr. Shah recommends wavelengths between 630 and 680 nanometers to successfully penetrate the scalp and stimulate hair follicle growth. If you have sensitive skin or are new to these tools, take it slow and work your way to the top level to limit irritation.

Dr. Bauman says that the 650-nanometer range is key, as it is the optimal wavelength absorbed by mitochondria for energy production to support hair follicle function. This process boosts cellular energy, as hair follicles are highly active structures that need a lot of energy to support the hair growth cycle. The end result is reduced inflammation, improved blood flow, and extended growth.

To be clear, no laser hair growth device is going to give you Thor-level flow overnight—these tools take time. Dr. Shah says that men will need at least six months of consistent use before seeing results after regular use. But not every device’s session will be the same. Some, you’ll need to wear or place near the dome for five minutes, while others for half an hour. Consider the comfort of your device, along with your schedule, before investing.

Most importantly, however, Dr. Shah says consistency is crucial because missing sessions, no matter how long they are, can reduce the device’s effectiveness. If executed properly, early results will appear around six months, such as reduced shedding or slight thickening, before fuller regrowth occurs near the one-year mark, according to Dr. Shah.

Whenever you’re dealing with new technology, rely on reputable organizations to first approve it for use. Both Dr. Shah and Dr. Bauman advise only looking to laser hair growth devices that have been accepted by the FDA for the safest, most effective experience. However, there are different levels of FDA acceptance. FDA-listed or FDA-registered simply means that the manufacturer has informed the FDA, but doesn’t imply approval or authorization.

FDA clearance, on the other hand, means the device is substantially equivalent to a product already on the market.

FDA approved is the ideal, as this means the device has successfully been through extensive testing and clinical trials to demonstrate safety and effectiveness. But to date, there have been no LED or laser diode devices for hair growth that are FDA-approved, so look for FDA-cleared options.

As someone whose hairline is still going strong after 33 years (and a ton of preventive hair thinning products), I leaned heavily on the counsel of hair loss professionals for these selections. I conferred with dermatologist Dr. Shah and hair restoration physician Dr. Bauman on what to look for in an effective laser hair growth device and which they recommend.

I also consulted with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors who have battled hair loss on their experience, based on ease of use, effectiveness, and long-term results. Following this research and testing, we nailed down these tools as the five best laser hair growth devices for men in 2026.

The app is available on iOS and Android. Early access began on iOS on Aug. 26, with Android early access following on Nov. 17 after the app attracted a waitlist of "tens of thousands of people," according to Aave Labs.

"Aave App makes the benefits of onchain finance accessible to everyday users, creating a better way to save," Aave Labs founder and CEO Stani Kulechov said. "The industry is at an important moment. The technologies that power onchain finance have finally come together in a way that allows the complexity to fade into the background."

Plans for the app were initially unveiled last November. At the time, Aave advertised rates of up to 9% and "insurance-backed protection" on deposits of up to $1 million. Aave Labs sought $5 million from the Aave DAO for the Aave App in February.

At public launch, Aave App offers verified users a variable 6% base rate for 90 days on balances of up to $100,000, Aave Labs said, adding that eligible users can lift that to 7.25% through referrals and recurring deposits. Users can withdraw without a penalty, while earnings accrue from the time of deposit and compound every second, according to the firm, though it noted that eligibility and availability vary by market.

Eligible users in the U.S., excluding New York, can move money between their bank accounts and Aave App through licensed third-party providers, including Bridge and Astra. Push by Aave Labs provides the same connection in the UK and EEA, according to the statement. Users in other supported jurisdictions can deposit USDC, USDT, or GHO stablecoins from eight networks: Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, BNB Chain, HyperEVM, Monad, Optimism, and TRON. Aave Labs said it will continue to expand bank connectivity as licensing and banking partnerships allow.

Deposits are supplied to lending markets on the Aave Protocol, the largest onchain lending protocol by total value locked, where borrower interest payments generate earnings for savers. The Aave Protocol uses an overcollateralized lending model, meaning borrowers deposit assets worth more than they borrow. Aave App’s Stable Vaults allocate funds among supported markets under preset rules, meaning users see a single savings balance without needing to manage stablecoins, networks, or lending markets themselves.

The app's discretionary Balance Protection program may reimburse eligible users for certain losses tied to security incidents, technology failures, and extended account lockouts, subject to its terms, Aave Labs said. Lockton placed supporting insurance arrangements with Relm Insurance, with part of the risk reinsured by Munich Re, but users do not hold insurance under the program. However, funds in Aave App are not bank deposits or covered by FDIC or SIPC insurance.

Aave Labs said it expects to expand the platform with additional financial products and capabilities over time.

#5040. South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade

South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade

South Korea is proposing to end its nine-year ban on initial coin offerings, a move aimed at pulling crypto fundraising back onshore, creating jobs and folding token sales into a regulated framework.

The country’s Financial Services Commission unveiled a draft bill, the Act on Digital Asset Industry Innovation and User Protection, on Tuesday that would reverse the prohibition imposed in September 2017, when regulators banned ICOs over fraud, speculation and investor losses.

If passed, it would let domestic projects issue and sell tokens to the public for the first time in nearly a decade.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Under the proposal, any issuer would have to file a “digital asset white paper” with the FSC before selling tokens, detailing the project, how the raised funds will be used, how many tokens will be issued and the risks involved. Issuers and their executives would face civil damages, financial penalties and possible criminal prosecution for false or omitted information, a liability regime modeled on the disclosure rules governing stock offerings.

The ban, regulators have concluded, never really worked. It largely pushed Korean projects to set up entities abroad and run their token sales through them, with game developers Wemade and Netmarble among the better-known firms that took the offshore route. The FSC’s stated goal is to reclaim that activity and the investment and jobs that went with it.

The ICO reversal is one piece of a sweeping overhaul. The same bill would restrict issuance of Korean won-backed stablecoins to consortiums in which commercial banks hold a majority stake, cap any single major shareholder’s ownership of a crypto exchange at 20% (rising to 34% under certain conditions), extend market-manipulation rules to crypto-to-crypto trades, and organize the market into regulated verticals spanning exchanges, trading, brokerage, custody and asset management.

The shift fits a broader global move toward regulated token fundraising, as the U.S. and others build out frameworks that give crypto issuers clearer legal footing. It also marks a notable turn for South Korea, one of the world’s most active retail crypto markets, which has long paired enthusiastic trading with strict rules.

The proposal is only a draft. It now heads to the National Assembly, where lawmakers must approve it before any of the changes take effect, leaving the timeline, and the final shape of the rules, still to be determined.

#5038. You Can See Everything You Ever Want to See in a Movie in You Can See Everything

Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary is three hours long. You’ll wish it went on for three more.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

NATHAN FIELDER HAS become one of the greatest arbiters of what is—or isn’t—the truth. Fielder, whose mainstream career unofficially kicked off with his show Nathan for You, a dry, quasi-documentary, quasi-scripted, quasi-spoof of shows like Undercover Boss, has found a way to level up with each project he’s made over the course of his still relatively short career, each step of the way inviting audiences to not only question the reality of what he’s bringing to the screen, but their own stances and ways of thinking about things broadly.

The road for Fielder has included HBO’s The Rehearsal (another often surreal, often Lynchian project that presents as real, but on a subtextual level asks viewers to question whether any of what he’s depicting was really happening as it was shown) and The Curse, a Showtime/Paramount+ series that he starred in and co-created alongside Emma Stone and Benny Safdie. That show was, surprise, surprise, incredibly thoughtful, layered, and, ultimately, surreal when it comes to its underlying themes of sincerity and intention.

In a way, all of this has led Fielder to his latest project, the new A24 documentary You Can See Everything. The subject is a fitting one for Fielder: Elizabeth Holmes, the former Theranos CEO and convicted fraudster who was the subject of books (Bad Blood) and television shows (The Dropout) about her misdeeds. It makes total sense that someone famous for skirting the truth would be of interest for Fielder, a creator who has now spent so much time examining not only the truth, but what audiences might accept as the truth even given some reason not to.

In 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison. That’s where You Can See Everything comes in: Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invited Fielder (and a film crew, led by co-director Lance Oppenheim) to join them in a home they were renting for complete access during the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in Bryan, Texas, in May 2023. And the film begins there.

And, quite frankly, if you’re considering seeing You Can See Everything, it’s best to leave it there. Fielder gets the access he was promised in the movie, but the joy of the film isn’t only in this exclusive vision of such a notable figure, but how an artist with such a relationship to the truth engages with someone who so notably has, seemingly, bent it. We also get to see Holmes and Evans shot as human beings, removed from any of the prior media circuses that have surrounded them. Fielder and Oppenheim put a fair camera to everything and let the camera do what was promised: See everything.

You Can See Everything has been one of the best-reviewed films of the year, and it lives up to the billing. Just when you think you understand what’s happening and what’s going to happen, you’ll be quickly proven wrong. Just when you think you have a handle on who someone is and what they’re all about… you’ll quickly be proven wrong. The movie is three hours long, which, of course, we know, seems daunting. But by the time it ends, you’ll wish it was going on for three hours more.

Below, we answer some of your questions about You Can See Everything—without spoiling any of the movie’s major twists or turns.

You Can See Everything is now available to watch at home. You can purchase it on Apple TV and rent it on Prime Video—and we suggest doing whichever of those you prefer.

You Can See Everything is, in essence, two movies in one. The first half of the movie is what the trailer and promotional materials for the movie billed: Nathan Fielder joins Elizabeth Holmes (and her new husband Billy Evans) in a home they rented for the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in 2023. This proves to be just as compelling as you’d imagine, as Holmes and Evans are both completely idiosyncratic characters. Moments like when Fielder shows Holmes Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First” bit are instant classics.

Eventually Holmes reports to prison in Bryan, Texas, and the movie is not even halfway over. It’s at this point that your eyebrow should raise, and you do the ‘leaning forward in seat’ meme—because this is when You Can See Everything gets truly wild. The timeline jumps forward two hours, and Nathan Fielder gets up to some of his mind-bending, Rehearsal-type business. At this point, we see some people’s true colors, and also meet some other unexpected guests and surprises in the movie. This second part of the movie is what will blow your mind, and leave you thinking long after the credits begin to roll.

You Can See Everything should be an absolute lock for a number of Oscar nominations, including Best Picture. And it should be a strong contender in one of the acting categories for one person whose appearance we will not be spoiling in this story.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim are the co-directors of You Can See Everything, and both have been key figures in American film and television culture for the last decade.

Fielder is a Canadian-born actor and director (and childhood friend of Seth Rogen) who rose to fame as the creator and star of Comedy Central’s Nathan for You. He’s dabbled in acting here and there—including a role as a limo driver in Rogen’s underrated holiday comedy The Night Before and in the sensational limited series The Curse—but his real calling has come in mind-bending documentary/comedy series like The Rehearsal. In season 2 of The Rehearsal, for example, Fielder actually got his pilot’s license while exploring the aviation industry. (And that was filmed between part 1 and part 2 of You Can See Everything, which is just bananas.)

Oppenheim, who is only 30, has also established himself as one of the best documentarians in the business. His movies Some Kind of Heaven and Spermworld along with his HBO series Ren Faire are deeply layered portrayals of very real people in very real situations; he shoots these documentaries in styles completely different from anyone else, though, lighting them like cinematic spectacles rather than what you probably think of as a documentary in your mind. (Some of the cinematography in You Can See Everything is unbelievably beautiful.)

Primetime, A24’s film about Chris Hansen and To Catch a Predator that came out last month and starred Robert Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo, and Merritt Wever, was Oppenheim’s scripted feature debut.

It probably helps to have information on Elizabeth Holmes’s case—which we recommend getting from any number of sources: The Dropout was the name of the Hulu series that starred Amanda Seyfried as Holmes, but it was also a well-researched and reported podcast that served as the show’s basis. There’s also an HBO documentary called The Inventor and a book called Bad Blood. Any of this would make for a good source for the crimes Holmes was accused of committing. The movie also includes a very brief recap of her case in the early going—not exhaustive, but enough to get the idea.

It does also make sense to have an idea of who Fielder is, what he does, and how he engages with his subjects. We recommend HBO’s The Rehearsal for that, but it’s not 100 percent necessary to enjoy and appreciate the film.

That’s the question, isn’t it? You Can See Everything explores the idea of truth, lies, perspective, and even documentary filmmaking itself. If it makes the most sense to you to take all of You Can See Everything at face value, then please go for it. If you feel the need to question everything, well, that’s okay too. That’s what makes Fielder’s work so unique and so immersive—you can think about it about 100 different ways, and no understanding or interpretation is wrong. It’s set up to feel like a kaleidoscope. You can understand something one way, but maybe something pops up, and suddenly you can’t think about it that way anymore. That’s the point—and that’s what you’ll think about long after the credits roll.

#5035. What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

The U.S. derivatives regulator has quietly opened the door for crypto exchanges and clearinghouses to hold Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins as part of the financial cushion they’re required to keep, the latest sign of the agency weaving digital assets into the plumbing of regulated markets.

But the fine print matters, and it draws a careful line.

In a staff advisory issued this week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk explained how swap execution facilities, designated contract markets, and derivatives clearing organizations can use crypto assets to meet their financial-resources requirements.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Those rules require such platforms to hold enough resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs, a buffer meant to ensure a venue can keep running or wind down safely if it hits trouble.

Here’s what the guidance allows: Certain crypto assets, specifically naming Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins, can now count toward that 12-month requirement, subject to “appropriate haircuts,” meaning their value would be discounted to account for volatility. That’s a meaningful concession, effectively recognizing crypto as a legitimate corporate reserve asset for the firms the CFTC oversees.

Here’s what it doesn’t allow, and this is the catch that defines the policy: Crypto can’t be counted toward a separate liquidity requirement.

Because digital assets don’t qualify as “cash” or “highly liquid securities” under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, they fall short of that stricter test. In practice, a platform can hold Bitcoin or Ethereum as part of its longer-term financial backstop, but it still needs traditional cash-like instruments on hand to satisfy the rule meant to ensure it can pay obligations quickly.

The distinction is the whole point. It lets firms treat crypto as a store of value on their balance sheets while reinforcing that, when it comes to assets that must be instantly spendable, volatile tokens still don’t make the cut.

The nuance is easy to miss, but it reflects a measured posture from a regulator that has otherwise moved aggressively on crypto.

The CFTC has already previously cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, issued no-action relief letting crypto apps offer regulated derivatives, and floated a plan to bring crypto exchanges under federal oversight, part of a broader push to set digital-asset policy on its own authority.

That said, it’s worth noting that the advisory represents the views of CFTC staff only. It creates no new rules or enforceable rights, isn’t a no-action position, and doesn’t necessarily reflect the views of the Commission itself.

It could also shift as the agency’s makeup changes. President Donald Trump recently sent a bipartisan slate of nominees to fill vacant CFTC and SEC seats, which could reshape the commissions now steering crypto policy.

For now, the guidance is best read not as crypto winning blanket acceptance as a reserve asset, but as the CFTC sorting out precisely where digital assets fit, and where they still don’t, in the machinery of regulated trading.

Bitcoin Losses Are the Worst Since FTX. Is the Bottom Near?

Bitcoin investors are locking in their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX in November 2022, according to a report published Tuesday by blockchain analytics firm Glassnode.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency slipped below $60,000, trading at $59,992, more than 50% from its October 2025 peak.

“Bitcoin losses are the heaviest since FTX,” Glassnode wrote on X. “Set against the money that flowed into Bitcoin over the past year, they have almost doubled in a week.”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Glassnode tracks realized losses by looking at coins that move on-chain at prices lower than when they previously moved. Measuring those losses against the capital that entered Bitcoin over the preceding year gives analysts a way to compare sell-offs across market cycles, even as the cryptocurrency grows in value.

The last time the indicator reached these levels, Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto empire was collapsing and Bitcoin was trading below $16,000. This time, the selling pressure has coincided with a much broader retreat from risky assets, and even good news for the tech industry hasn’t been enough to keep Bitcoin afloat.

Bitcoin rallied 5% in about half an hour on Monday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO. Less than six hours later, Bitcoin had given back the entire rally, while the Nasdaq 100 still held roughly three-quarters of its gains. In trading, this is known as a bull trap, and happens on strong bearish trends.

Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq 100 is now at its highest since September 2022, Glassnode said. Over the past 60 trading days, Bitcoin has tended to gain less when tech stocks rise and lose more when they fall.

U.S. investors have also been pulling money out of the market. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $4.3 billion on net over the past 20 trading days, while Coinbase traders have been heavy net sellers over the past month. Buying and selling on Binance, meanwhile, have been roughly balanced.

“Spikes like this often came close to past lows, but some came early,” Glassnode said. The firm pointed to the sell-offs of early 2019, March 2020, and November 2022, when losses surged near market bottoms, but also to earlier episodes in 2018 and 2022 when prices had further to fall.

Long-term holders—investors who have held their coins for roughly five months or longer—accounted for most realized losses from mid-April to mid-November. Nearly 90% of the long futures positions vulnerable to liquidation between last week’s Bitcoin price and $53,200 are also gone, reducing the potential for another cascade of forced selling within that range.

Glassnode is watching Bitcoin’s realized price, the average price at which circulating coins last moved, which currently stands at $53,200. Bitcoin traded below that metric before bottoming in each of the previous three major bear markets.

Applying the discounts seen at the lows of 2022 and 2018 to today’s realized price would put Bitcoin at roughly $41,000 and $37,000, respectively.

For now, the more immediate concern is whether Bitcoin can close above its June closing low of $58,500. Glassnode said a recovery above $60,000 accompanied by renewed ETF inflows would help establish whether the summer lows are holding.

#5021. Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

The 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and new. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

Lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

Those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone shows, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

The adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

The road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

This progression from an exciting new technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

One case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured big personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

In both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the new, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too big to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

People investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire company is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

The main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the new cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news shows. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

Fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening new possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

You know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

When revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building new financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

What we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous new things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too big to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

Even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a new one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉

#5019. Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing

Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled the size of its protocol security team and made strengthening Ethereum's cryptography its highest priority, warning that artificial intelligence could undermine the mathematical foundations of the network before quantum computers get powerful enough to do so.

"The EF has been planning mitigations to the threat posed by quantum computers," Kev Wedderburn wrote in a blog post published Monday, adding that "recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk."

For years, the crypto industry has worried about Q-Day—the hypothetical moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break the cryptography protecting digital assets. AI introduces a different problem: What if someone discovers a mathematical shortcut that makes such a machine unnecessary?

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Ethereum with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Bitcoin and Ethereum both rely on elliptic curve cryptography to authenticate transactions. Its security depends on mathematical problems that are relatively easy to solve in one direction but prohibitively difficult to reverse using known algorithms.

An AI capable of discovering substantially better algorithms could change that equation without requiring any breakthroughs in quantum hardware.

Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake raised this possibility in October, warning that existing signature schemes could become vulnerable within months rather than years under a worst-case scenario. He recommended that the industry start preparing for an orderly migration of funds to addresses whose public keys have never been exposed.

The Foundation's latest announcement comes just days after Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and Claude produced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had remained unsolved since 1859.

The proof does not break Bitcoin or Ethereum's cryptography, but it illustrates how quickly AI is becoming useful in areas of mathematics previously considered beyond its capabilities.

The bug had survived roughly four years of scrutiny by cryptographers.

Ethereum's proposed solution involves moving away from elliptic curves and adopting hash-based cryptography. Hash functions turn data into fixed-length digital fingerprints that are designed to be extremely difficult to reverse, and their security relies on fewer structural mathematical assumptions than elliptic curve schemes.

Ethereum already depends on secure hash functions, making them an attractive foundation for its new security architecture.

The transition would affect how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how Ethereum verifies data submitted by layer-2 networks.

Developers are also pursuing formal verification, a technique that uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that software behaves according to its specifications. Ironically, AI could help accelerate that work.

The Foundation has been deploying AI agents against its own infrastructure since earlier this year, successfully identifying software vulnerabilities before malicious actors could exploit them.

The security overhaul comes at a cost. Ethereum developers will need to rethink some planned features, and larger cryptographic signatures could increase hardware requirements for people running their own nodes.

Development group Ethlabs has already withdrawn its proposal to introduce faster block production in the upcoming Hegotá upgrade, freeing up engineering resources to pursue an ambitious target of making Ethereum resistant to both threats in 2027.

The Foundation previously established December 2029 as its internal deadline for achieving quantum resistance across Ethereum's base layer. Drake proposed bringing that target forward to December 2028 at the recent Devcon conference in Mumbai.

The Foundation plans to reassess its timeline in January 2027, with developers already testing early implementations of the new cryptographic infrastructure.

Anchorage Digital Bank, BitGo Bank & Trust and Coinbase Custody would serve as custodians for the fund's LINK. Authorized participants would be able to create and redeem large blocks of ETF shares using either LINK or cash. The filing does not mention when the fund could begin trading.

Grayscale and Bitwise already offer U.S. spot Chainlink ETFs. As of Nov. 24, the Grayscale Chainlink Trust ETF (GLNK) had about $112 million in assets under management, and the Bitwise Chainlink ETF (CLNK) had about $42 million.

Fidelity currently offers three spot crypto ETFs in the U.S. covering bitcoin, ether, and Solana. These include the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), the Fidelity Ethereum Fund (FETH), and the Fidelity Solana Fund (FSOL). Unlike the proposed Chainlink fund, Fidelity's Solana fund, which began trading in November 2025, stakes its tokens.

The Chainlink ETF filing comes a day after Fidelity expanded the number of cryptocurrencies available for trading on its Fidelity Crypto platform, adding Chainlink's LINK, Aave's AAVE, and Uniswap's UNI.

Fidelity also entered the stablecoin market earlier this year, launching its first U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin, Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD), on Ethereum in February.
